(c) \(E\) is rank 1 with single singular value \(\sigma_2\), so \(\lVert E \rVert_2 = \lVert E \rVert_F = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\). Directly: \(\lVert E \rVert_F^2 = 2.25 + 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 = 5\). The fraction kept is

\[ \frac{\sigma_1^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2} = \frac{45}{50} = \mathbf{90\%}. \]

(d) \(A^\top A = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 14 \\ 14 & 20 \end{bmatrix}\), with \(\lambda^2 - 30\lambda + 4 = 0\), so \(\lambda = 15 \pm \sqrt{221}\) and

\[ \lVert A \rVert_2 = \sigma_1 = \sqrt{15 + \sqrt{221}} \approx \mathbf{5.465}, \qquad \sigma_2 = \sqrt{15 - \sqrt{221}} \approx 0.366, \]

matching slide 201 (and \(\sigma_1\sigma_2 = \sqrt{225 - 221} = 2 = \lvert \det A \rvert\)).

Key insight: The error of a truncated SVD is itself an SVD, built from the discarded terms, so its norms can be read straight off the discarded singular values.

P5.22 L3 · Application

Rank-\(k\) approximations of a \(4 \times 3\) matrix

The matrix

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 6 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 11 \\ 5 & 10 & 1 \\ -3 & 6 & 9 \end{bmatrix} \]

has the (thin) SVD \(A = \sum_{i=1}^{3} \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top\) with \(\sigma = (18, 12, 6)\) and

\[ u_1 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1, 1, 1, 1)^\top, \quad u_2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1, -1, 1, -1)^\top, \quad u_3 = \tfrac{1}{2}(1, 1, -1, -1)^\top, \]

\[ v_1 = \tfrac{1}{3}(1, 2, 2)^\top, \quad v_2 = \tfrac{1}{3}(2, 1, -2)^\top, \quad v_3 = \tfrac{1}{3}(2, -2, 1)^\top. \]

(a) Check that the \(u\)'s and the \(v\)'s are orthonormal, and that \(Av_1 = \sigma_1 u_1\).

(b) Compute \(\hat{A}(1)\) and \(\hat{A}(2)\).

(c) Give \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_2\) and \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_F\) for \(k = 1, 2\), and verify one of them by direct computation.

(d) What fraction of \(\lVert A \rVert_F^2\) does each approximation keep? Check \(\lVert A \rVert_F^2\) from the entries.

(e) How many numbers are needed to store \(\hat{A}(2)\)? Is it a saving for this matrix?

Hint

Each \(u_i v_i^\top\) has entries \(\pm\tfrac{1}{6}\) or \(\pm\tfrac{2}{6}\), so \(\sigma_i u_i v_i^\top\) has integer entries here.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Each \(u_i\) has length \(\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{4} = 1\) and each \(v_i\) has length \(\tfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{9} = 1\). Pairwise dot products, e.g. \(u_1 \cdot u_2 = \tfrac{1}{4}(1 - 1 + 1 - 1) = 0\) and \(v_1 \cdot v_2 = \tfrac{1}{9}(2 + 2 - 4) = 0\), all vanish. And

\[ Av_1 = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 9 + 12 + 6 \\ 1 + 4 + 22 \\ 5 + 20 + 2 \\ -3 + 12 + 18 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 9 \\ 9 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix} = 18 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}(1, 1, 1, 1)^\top. \ \checkmark \]

(b)

\[ \hat{A}(1) = 18 u_1 v_1^\top = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 6 & 6 \\ 3 & 6 & 6 \\ 3 & 6 & 6 \\ 3 & 6 & 6 \end{bmatrix}}, \qquad 12 u_2 v_2^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 & -4 \\ -4 & -2 & 4 \\ 4 & 2 & -4 \\ -4 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \hat{A}(2) = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 7 & 8 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 & 10 \\ 7 & 8 & 2 \\ -1 & 4 & 10 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

(c)

\[ \begin{aligned} k = 1:&\quad \lVert A - \hat{A}(1) \rVert_2 = \sigma_2 = \mathbf{12}, & \lVert A - \hat{A}(1) \rVert_F &= \sqrt{12^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{180} = \mathbf{6\sqrt{5} \approx 13.416}, \\ k = 2:&\quad \lVert A - \hat{A}(2) \rVert_2 = \sigma_3 = \mathbf{6}, & \lVert A - \hat{A}(2) \rVert_F &= \mathbf{6}. \end{aligned} \]

Direct check for \(k = 2\): \(A - \hat{A}(2) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = 6u_3v_3^\top\), whose squared entries sum to \(4 \times 9 = 36\).

(d) \(\lVert A \rVert_F^2 = 18^2 + 12^2 + 6^2 = 324 + 144 + 36 = 504\), which matches the sum of the squared entries \((81 + 36 + 9) + (1 + 4 + 121) + (25 + 100 + 1) + (9 + 36 + 81) = 504\).

\[ \hat{A}(1): \ \frac{324}{504} = \frac{9}{14} \approx \mathbf{64.3\%}, \qquad \hat{A}(2): \ \frac{468}{504} = \frac{13}{14} \approx \mathbf{92.9\%}. \]

(e) \(k(m + n + 1) = 2(4 + 3 + 1) = \mathbf{16}\) numbers, against \(4 \times 3 = 12\) for \(A\) itself: no saving. Truncation only saves storage when \(k < \frac{mn}{m + n + 1}\), here \(k < 1.5\).

Key insight: The spectral error is the first dropped singular value and the Frobenius error is the root-sum-square of all dropped ones; storage savings appear only for matrices much larger than their effective rank.

P5.23 L4 · Analysis

Proving that the spectral norm is the largest singular value

Let \(A = U\Sigma V^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) with singular values \(\sigma_1 \ge \dots \ge \sigma_r > 0\).

(a) Prove the theorem of slide 200: \(\lVert A \rVert_2 = \max_{x \ne 0} \lVert Ax \rVert_2 / \lVert x \rVert_2 = \sigma_1\), and say which \(x\) attains the maximum.

(b) For \(n \le m\), prove that \(\min_{x \ne 0} \lVert Ax \rVert_2 / \lVert x \rVert_2 = \sigma_n\) (with \(\sigma_n = 0\) if \(r < n\)).

(c) Deduce \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_2 = \sigma_{k+1}\).

(d) Prove \(\lVert A \rVert_F^2 = \sum_i \sigma_i^2\), and deduce \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2}\).

(e) What breaks if one uses the largest \(\lvert \lambda \rvert\) instead of \(\sigma_1\) as the "size" of a square matrix? Give two examples.

Hint

Orthogonal matrices preserve lengths. Substitute \(y = V^\top x\), so \(\lVert y \rVert = \lVert x \rVert\) and \(\lVert Ax \rVert = \lVert \Sigma y \rVert\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Let \(y = V^\top x\); then \(\lVert y \rVert_2 = \lVert x \rVert_2\) and, since \(U\) preserves lengths,

\[ \lVert Ax \rVert_2^2 = \lVert U\Sigma y \rVert_2^2 = \lVert \Sigma y \rVert_2^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^2 y_i^2 \le \sigma_1^2 \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i^2 = \sigma_1^2 \lVert x \rVert_2^2. \]

So \(\lVert Ax \rVert_2 / \lVert x \rVert_2 \le \sigma_1\) for every \(x \ne 0\), and \(x = v_1\) (\(y = e_1\)) gives \(\lVert Av_1 \rVert_2 = \lVert \sigma_1 u_1 \rVert_2 = \sigma_1\). Hence \(\lVert A \rVert_2 = \sigma_1\).

(b) With \(n \le m\), \(\Sigma\) has \(n\) diagonal positions \(\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_n\) (zeros beyond \(r\)), and \(\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sigma_i^2 y_i^2 \ge \sigma_n^2 \lVert y \rVert^2\), with equality at \(x = v_n\). So the minimum stretch is \(\sigma_n\).

(c) \(A - \hat{A}(k) = \sum_{i=k+1}^{r} \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top = U \Sigma' V^\top\), where \(\Sigma'\) is \(\Sigma\) with its first \(k\) diagonal entries set to zero. This is an SVD (after reordering) whose largest singular value is \(\sigma_{k+1}\), so by (a) \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_2 = \sigma_{k+1}\).

(d) For orthogonal \(Q\), \(\lVert QM \rVert_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(M^\top Q^\top Q M) = \operatorname{tr}(M^\top M) = \lVert M \rVert_F^2\), and likewise \(\lVert MQ \rVert_F = \lVert M \rVert_F\). So

\[ \lVert A \rVert_F^2 = \lVert U \Sigma V^\top \rVert_F^2 = \lVert \Sigma \rVert_F^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \sigma_i^2, \]

and applying the same identity to \(U\Sigma'V^\top\) gives \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_F = \sqrt{\sigma_{k+1}^2 + \dots + \sigma_r^2}\).

(e) The largest \(\lvert \lambda \rvert\) (the spectral radius) is not a norm and can badly underestimate how much \(A\) stretches:

  • \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) has both eigenvalues \(0\) but sends \(e_2\) to \(e_1\), so \(\sigma_1 = 1\). A non-zero matrix would have "size" zero.
  • \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) (P5.19) has \(\max \lvert \lambda \rvert = 5\) but \(\lVert A \rVert_2 = \sqrt{10} + \sqrt{5} \approx 5.398\).

For symmetric matrices the two agree, because then \(\sigma_i = \lvert \lambda_i \rvert\).

Key insight: Because \(U\) and \(V\) are rigid motions, every length-based question about \(A\) (largest stretch, smallest stretch, Frobenius size, truncation error) reduces to the same question about the diagonal \(\Sigma\).

P5.24 L4 · Analysis

Eckart–Young: why truncation is the best you can do

(a) State the Eckart–Young theorem for the spectral norm and for the Frobenius norm.

(b) Prove the spectral-norm version: for every \(B\) with \(\operatorname{rank} B \le k < r\), \(\lVert A - B \rVert_2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}\).

(c) For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) (P5.14, P5.21), compare the error of the SVD rank-1 truncation with two "obvious" rank-1 approximations: keep only column 2, and keep only row 2.

(d) What breaks if \(\sigma_k = \sigma_{k+1}\)? Illustrate with \(I_2\) and \(k = 1\).

Hint

For (b), \(\operatorname{null}(B)\) has dimension at least \(n - k\), and \(\operatorname{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_{k+1}\}\) has dimension \(k + 1\). Two subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) whose dimensions add up to more than \(n\) must share a non-zero vector.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Eckart–Young. For \(k < r\), the truncation \(\hat{A}(k) = \sum_{i \le k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^\top\) solves \(\min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k} \lVert A - B \rVert\) in both norms, with minimum values

\[ \min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k} \lVert A - B \rVert_2 = \sigma_{k+1}, \qquad \min_{\operatorname{rank} B \le k} \lVert A - B \rVert_F = \sqrt{\sum_{i > k} \sigma_i^2}. \]

(b) Let \(\operatorname{rank} B \le k\). By rank–nullity \(\dim \operatorname{null}(B) \ge n - k\). The subspace \(W = \operatorname{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_{k+1}\}\) has dimension \(k + 1\), and \((n - k) + (k + 1) > n\), so there is a unit vector \(w \in W \cap \operatorname{null}(B)\). Write \(w = \sum_{i \le k+1} c_i v_i\) with \(\sum c_i^2 = 1\). Then

\[ \lVert (A - B) w \rVert_2^2 = \lVert Aw \rVert_2^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} \sigma_i^2 c_i^2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}^2 \sum_{i=1}^{k+1} c_i^2 = \sigma_{k+1}^2, \]

so \(\lVert A - B \rVert_2 \ge \sigma_{k+1}\). P5.23(c) shows that \(\hat{A}(k)\) attains this bound, so it is optimal.

(c)

Rank-1 candidate \(B\) \(A - B\) \(\lVert A - B \rVert_2\) \(\lVert A - B \rVert_F\)
SVD truncation \(\tfrac{3}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) \(\tfrac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\) \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\)
keep column 2: \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) \(5\) \(5\)
keep row 2: \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) \(3\) \(3\)

The SVD truncation wins in both norms, at \(\sigma_2 = \sqrt{5}\), and no other rank-1 matrix can do better.

(d) The optimal value \(\sigma_{k+1}\) is still correct, but the minimiser is no longer unique. For \(I_2\), \(\sigma_1 = \sigma_2 = 1\), and every \(B = qq^\top\) with \(q\) a unit vector gives \(I - qq^\top = pp^\top\) (\(p \perp q\)), with error exactly 1 in both norms. "The" rank-\(k\) approximation is well defined only when \(\sigma_k > \sigma_{k+1}\); in practice a near-tie makes the leading singular vectors numerically unstable.

Key insight: A rank-\(k\) matrix must ignore some \((n-k)\)-dimensional set of input directions, and that set always meets the top \(k+1\) right singular directions, so at least \(\sigma_{k+1}\) of stretch is lost; the SVD loses exactly that and nothing more.

7.G Module 5 Capstone

P5.25 L5 · Mastery

Compressing an image with a truncated SVD

A grayscale image is stored as a matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{600 \times 800}\) of pixel intensities. Its five largest singular values are

\[ \sigma_1 = 120, \quad \sigma_2 = 60, \quad \sigma_3 = 30, \quad \sigma_4 = 20, \quad \sigma_5 = 10, \]

and the remaining 595 singular values (all \(\le 10\)) satisfy \(\sum_{i=6}^{600} \sigma_i^2 = 600\).

(a) How many numbers does it take to store \(A\), and to store \(\hat{A}(k)\)? Give the counts for \(k = 4\), \(20\) and \(50\) as a fraction of the original.

(b) Above which \(k\) does the truncated SVD stop saving storage?

(c) Compute \(\lVert A \rVert_F^2\) and the fraction of "energy" \(\sum_{i \le k} \sigma_i^2 / \sum_i \sigma_i^2\) kept for \(k = 1, \dots, 5\). What is the smallest \(k\) that keeps at least 95%?

(d) For that \(k\), give the worst-case error \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_2\) and the relative Frobenius error \(\lVert A - \hat{A}(k) \rVert_F / \lVert A \rVert_F\).

(e) A colleague says: "Keeping 96.5% of the energy means 96.5% of the pixels are reproduced exactly." Correct this. Also say how the storage count changes for an RGB image compressed channel by channel.

Hint

Each rank-1 term costs \(m + n + 1\) numbers. Energy is measured by \(\lVert \cdot \rVert_F^2 = \sum \sigma_i^2\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(A\) needs \(mn = 600 \times 800 = 480\,000\) numbers; \(\hat{A}(k)\) needs \(k(m + n + 1) = 1401k\).

\(k\) numbers stored fraction of \(480\,000\)
4 5604 1.17%
20 28,020 5.84%
50 70,050 14.6%

(b) Saving requires \(1401k < 480\,000\), i.e. \(k < 342.6\). For \(k \ge 343\) the truncation costs more than the raw image.

(c) \(\lVert A \rVert_F^2 = 14\,400 + 3600 + 900 + 400 + 100 + 600 = \mathbf{20\,000}\).

\(k\) \(\sum_{i \le k} \sigma_i^2\) energy kept
1 14,400 72.0%
2 18,000 90.0%
3 18,900 94.5%
4 19,300 96.5%
5 19,400 97.0%

The smallest \(k\) reaching 95% is \(k = 4\).

(d)

\[ \lVert A - \hat{A}(4) \rVert_2 = \sigma_5 = \mathbf{10}, \qquad \frac{\lVert A - \hat{A}(4) \rVert_F}{\lVert A \rVert_F} = \sqrt{\frac{700}{20\,000}} = \sqrt{0.035} \approx \mathbf{0.187}. \]

So 96.5% of the energy still leaves an 18.7% relative error in Frobenius norm, because the error norm is the square root of the lost energy fraction. Relative to the largest stretch, the worst-case error is \(10/120 \approx 8.3\%\).

(e) Energy is a sum of squares over the whole matrix; it says nothing about individual pixels. In general no pixel is reproduced exactly: the error \(A - \hat{A}(4)\) is spread over all entries, with \(\sum_{ij}(\text{error})^2 = 700\), about \(0.0015\) per pixel on average. What 96.5% means is that the discarded rank-1 layers carry 3.5% of the squared intensity. For RGB, each of the three channels gets its own SVD, so storage is \(3k(m + n + 1)\) against \(3mn\); the fractions in (a) are unchanged.

Key insight: A truncated SVD is the best rank-\(k\) image in the squared-error sense (Eckart–Young), but "best" is measured in energy, and the relative error is the square root of the energy lost, so a high percentage of energy can still mean visible blur.

P5.26 L5 · Mastery

A rating matrix and its latent factors

Four users rate three films (rows are users, columns are films; 0 means "not rated"):

\[ R = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 & 0 \\ 5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(a) Compute \(R^\top R\) and its eigenvalues, and hence the singular values of \(R\).

(b) Find \(v_1, v_2\) and \(u_1 = Rv_1/\sigma_1\), \(u_2 = Rv_2/\sigma_2\). Interpret \(u_1\) and \(v_1\) as a "latent factor".

(c) Compute the rank-1 approximation \(R_1\) and its errors in both norms. What fraction of \(\lVert R \rVert_F^2\) does it keep?

(d) A fifth user rates film 1 with a 5 and nothing else. Assuming their rating row is a multiple of the factor \(v_1^\top\), predict their ratings of films 2 and 3.

(e) Explain why the prediction for film 3 in (d), and the whole use of a plain SVD here, is questionable. What do real recommender systems do instead?

Hint

\(R^\top R\) is block diagonal, and its top-left block \(\begin{bmatrix} 50 & 40 \\ 40 & 32 \end{bmatrix}\) is \(2\,(5, 4)^\top(5, 4)\), a rank-1 matrix.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ R^\top R = \begin{bmatrix} 50 & 40 & 0 \\ 40 & 32 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 18 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The top-left block \(2\,(5, 4)^\top (5, 4)\) has eigenvalues \(2 \times 41 = 82\) (eigenvector \((5, 4)\)) and \(0\) (eigenvector \((4, -5)\)), and the last block gives \(18\). So the eigenvalues are \(82, 18, 0\) and

\[ \sigma_1 = \sqrt{82} \approx \mathbf{9.055}, \qquad \sigma_2 = \sqrt{18} = 3\sqrt{2} \approx \mathbf{4.243}, \qquad \operatorname{rank} R = 2. \]

(b) \(v_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{41}}(5, 4, 0)^\top\), \(v_2 = (0, 0, 1)^\top\) (and \(v_3 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{41}}(4, -5, 0)^\top\) spans \(\operatorname{null}(R)\)).

\[ u_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{82}} \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{41}}\begin{bmatrix} 41 \\ 41 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad u_2 = \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The first factor is a "taste" shared by films 1 and 2 (loadings \(5 : 4\) in \(v_1\)) and by users 1 and 2 (equal weights in \(u_1\)); call it genre A. The second factor is genre B: film 3 and users 3, 4. The SVD found the two taste groups without being told about genres.

(c)

\[ R_1 = \sigma_1 u_1 v_1^\top = \frac{\sqrt{82}}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{41}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 & 0 \\ 5 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

\(R - R_1\) is the genre-B block, a rank-1 matrix with singular value \(\sigma_2\), so \(\lVert R - R_1 \rVert_2 = \lVert R - R_1 \rVert_F = 3\sqrt{2} \approx 4.243\). Energy kept: \(\lVert R \rVert_F^2 = 25 + 16 + 25 + 16 + 9 + 9 = 100\), so \(82/100 = \mathbf{82\%}\). Note that \(R_1\) knows nothing at all about users 3 and 4.

(d) Their row is \(c\,(5, 4, 0)\); the film-1 rating gives \(5c = 5\), so \(c = 1\) and the prediction is film 2: 4, film 3: 0.

(e) The "0" for film 3 is not a prediction of dislike; it is an artefact of treating every unrated entry as a rating of 0. A plain SVD fits those zeros as if they were data, so it learns "genre-A fans rate genre-B films 0" from the absence of ratings. Practical recommenders (matrix factorisation, as popularised by the Netflix Prize) fit \(R \approx PQ^\top\) with rank \(k\) by minimising squared error over the observed entries only, usually with regularisation, and often after subtracting user and film means. The SVD remains the right picture of what a low-rank factor model is, and Eckart–Young is why rank-\(k\) truncation is the natural target when all entries are known.

Key insight: The leading singular vectors of a rating matrix are latent factors (a taste profile for films and an affinity score for users); the maths is exact, but the meaning of a zero entry decides whether the factors are trustworthy.

P5.27 L5 · Mastery

The pseudo-inverse and least squares

For \(A = U\Sigma V^\top\) of rank \(r\), the pseudo-inverse is

\[ A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^\top = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \frac{1}{\sigma_i} v_i u_i^\top, \]

where \(\Sigma^+ \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}\) is \(\Sigma^\top\) with each non-zero \(\sigma_i\) replaced by \(1/\sigma_i\).

(a) Use the SVD of \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) from P5.15 to compute \(A^+\), and check it against \((A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top\).

(b) Solve the least-squares problem \(\min_x \lVert Ax - b \rVert_2\) for \(b = (3, 1, 1)^\top\) with \(x = A^+b\). Show that the residual is orthogonal to the column space, and identify it with a singular vector.

(c) Now take the rank-1 matrix \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(b = (2, 0)^\top\). Why do the normal equations fail? Compute \(C^+\) and \(C^+b\), and explain which of the many least-squares solutions it picks.

(d) In linear regression with nearly collinear features, a design matrix has \(\sigma = (10, 0.001)\). Explain from the formula for \(A^+\) why the fitted weights are unstable, and describe one SVD-based fix.

Hint

For \(C\), \(C = 2uu^\top\) with \(u = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)^\top\). Every \(x\) with \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\) minimises \(\lVert Cx - b \rVert\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) From P5.15, \(\sigma = (\sqrt{3}, 1)\), \(v_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1)\), \(v_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, -1)\), \(u_1 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2, 1, 1)\), \(u_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(0, -1, 1)\). Then

\[ A^+ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} v_1 u_1^\top + \frac{1}{1} v_2 u_2^\top = \frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Check: \((A^\top A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \((A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\). The two agree because \(A\) has full column rank.

(b)

\[ x = A^+ b = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 3 - 1 + 2 \\ 3 + 2 - 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 4/3 \\ 4/3 \end{bmatrix}}, \qquad b - Ax = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 8/3 \\ 4/3 \\ 4/3 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The residual is \(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} u_3\), a multiple of the third left singular vector, which spans \(\operatorname{null}(A^\top)\); so \(A^\top(b - Ax) = 0\), the normal equations hold, and the residual is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{col}(A)\). Its length \(\lVert b - Ax \rVert = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) is the component of \(b\) along \(u_3\), the part no choice of \(x\) can reach.

(c) \(C^\top C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) is singular, so \((C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\) does not exist and \(C^\top C x = C^\top b\) has infinitely many solutions, the line \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\). With \(C = 2uu^\top\) (\(\sigma_1 = 2\), \(u_1 = v_1 = u\)):

\[ C^+ = \frac{1}{2} v_1 u_1^\top = \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad C^+ b = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ 1/2 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

\(C^+b\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{v_1, \dots, v_r\} = \operatorname{row}(C)\), with no component along \(\operatorname{null}(C)\); so among all least-squares solutions it is the one of minimum norm (\(\lVert x \rVert^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\), the smallest on the line \(x_1 + x_2 = 1\)).

(d) \(A^+ = \sum_i \sigma_i^{-1} v_i u_i^\top\) multiplies the component of \(b\) along \(u_2\) by \(1/\sigma_2 = 1000\). A tiny amount of noise in that direction becomes a huge swing in the weights along \(v_2\), the direction in which the two features cancel. Fixes: truncated SVD (drop terms with \(\sigma_i\) below a threshold, i.e. use \(\hat{A}(k)^+\)), or ridge regression, which replaces \(1/\sigma_i\) by \(\sigma_i/(\sigma_i^2 + \lambda)\), close to \(1/\sigma_i\) for large \(\sigma_i\) and close to \(0\) for tiny ones. The ratio \(\sigma_1/\sigma_r = 10^4\) (the condition number) is the warning sign.

Key insight: The pseudo-inverse inverts \(A\) on the directions it actually uses (dividing by each \(\sigma_i\)) and ignores the rest, which gives the least-squares solution of minimum norm; small singular values are exactly where that inversion becomes dangerous.

P5.28 L5 · Mastery

Six misconceptions about the SVD

Each statement below was written by a student. Say what is wrong (or right), and back your answer with a concrete matrix from this module.

(a) "Singular values are just the eigenvalues of \(A\)."

(b) "The SVD only works for square matrices, like the eigendecomposition."

(c) "OK, but for a symmetric matrix the singular values are the eigenvalues."

(d) "I took \(U\) from the eigenvectors of \(AA^\top\) and \(V\) from those of \(A^\top A\) for \(A = \operatorname{diag}(2, -3)\), and \(U\Sigma V^\top\) came out as \(\operatorname{diag}(2, 3)\). So this matrix has no SVD."

(e) "\(A^\top A\) is \(n \times n\) and \(AA^\top\) is \(m \times m\), so for a non-square \(A\) they have different non-zero eigenvalues, and it matters which one I use for the singular values."

(f) "To compress a matrix to rank \(k\), I set its smallest entries to zero."

Hint

Reuse P5.9, P5.14, P5.16, P5.18 and P5.24.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Wrong. \(\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i(A^\top A)}\). For \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) (P5.14) the eigenvalues are \(3, 5\) and the singular values \(3\sqrt{5} \approx 6.708\), \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\). For \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) the eigenvalues are \(0, 0\) but \(\sigma_1 = 1\).

(b) Wrong. The SVD exists for every \(m \times n\) matrix; P5.16 decomposes a \(2 \times 3\) matrix and P5.15 a \(3 \times 2\) one. It is the eigendecomposition that needs a square matrix with a full eigenbasis.

(c) Half right. For symmetric \(A\), \(\sigma_i = \lvert \lambda_i \rvert\), not \(\lambda_i\). \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\) (P5.18) has eigenvalues \(2, -3\) and singular values \(3, 2\). They coincide exactly only for symmetric positive semidefinite matrices.

(d) Wrong conclusion. Every matrix has an SVD. With \(AA^\top = A^\top A = \operatorname{diag}(4, 9)\), choosing \(U = V = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) gives \(U\Sigma V^\top = \operatorname{diag}(2, 3)\), because the two eigenvector computations chose their signs independently. Computing \(u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i\) instead gives \(u_1 = (0, -1)^\top\), \(u_2 = (1, 0)^\top\), and then \(U\Sigma V^\top = \operatorname{diag}(2, -3)\) (P5.9).

(e) Wrong. The non-zero eigenvalues of \(A^\top A\) and \(AA^\top\) are identical (P5.10(c)); only the number of extra zeros differs. In P5.16, \(AA^\top\) has eigenvalues \(9, 1\) and \(A^\top A\) has \(9, 1, 0\). Use whichever is smaller.

(f) Wrong. Zeroing entries neither controls the rank nor minimises the error. By Eckart–Young the best rank-\(k\) approximation drops the smallest singular values. In P5.24, keeping one column of \(\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\) gives error 5, keeping the SVD's first term gives \(\sqrt{5}\).

Key insight: Most SVD mistakes come from treating it as an eigendecomposition; it is the eigendecomposition of \(A^\top A\) and \(AA^\top\), stitched together by \(u_i = Av_i/\sigma_i\), and it lives on every rectangular matrix.

PART 8 — Module 6: Differentiation, Backpropagation & Automatic Differentiation

Conventions used throughout this module (they follow the Topic 6 and Topic 7 decks, slides 204–258). Gradient layout. For a scalar function \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) the gradient is a row vector, as on slide 218:

\[ \nabla_x f = \frac{df}{dx} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} & \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} & \cdots & \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}. \]

For \(f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m\) the Jacobian \(\frac{df}{dx} = J\) is \(m \times n\), with \(J_{ij} = \partial f_i / \partial x_j\) (row \(i\) is the gradient of \(f_i\), column \(j\) is \(\partial f / \partial x_j\)). With this layout the chain rule is a product of Jacobians in the order of the composition, \(\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial g}\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\), and the shapes must match. Many ML textbooks (and most code) use the column gradient \((\nabla_x f)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 1}\); in that layout the identities below are simply transposed, for example \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^\top A x) = x^\top(A + A^\top)\) (row) versus \((A + A^\top)x\) (column), and a gradient-descent step is \(x \leftarrow x - \gamma (\nabla_x f)^\top\). For a scalar function of a matrix \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial X}\) is the \(m \times n\) matrix of entries \(\partial f / \partial X_{ij}\) (same shape as \(X\)), as on slide 235. The sigmoid-layer derivation of slides 248–256 (section 8.G) is written in column layout: \(\delta^{(a)} = \partial \text{Loss}/\partial a\) and \(\delta^{(Z)} = \partial \text{Loss}/\partial Z\) are column vectors, so \(\partial \text{Loss}/\partial x = A^\top \delta^{(Z)}\) is a column. Every problem says which layout it uses. \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})\) is the sigmoid, \(\odot\) is the element-wise (Hadamard) product, \(\log\) is the natural log, and "finite-difference check" means the central difference \(\frac{f(x + h e_i) - f(x - h e_i)}{2h}\) unless stated otherwise. Slide slips handled inside the problems: slide 211 (Taylor coefficients not divided by \(k!\)), slide 221 (\(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\), not \(\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\)), slide 247 (\(\partial g_j / \partial x_i\), not \(\partial g_i / \partial x_i\)) and slide 239 (parameter indices run \(0, \dots, K-1\)).

8.A Univariate Differentiation (6.1)

P6.1 L1 · Foundation

Univariate differentiation: true or false

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "When we fit a linear-regression model by minimising a loss, we differentiate the loss with respect to the weights and treat the training data as constants."

(b) "The derivative \(\frac{df}{dx} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}\) only needs the limit as \(h\) approaches 0 from above."

(c) "If \(f'(x_0) < 0\), then moving a little to the left of \(x_0\) increases \(f\)."

(d) "The Taylor polynomial \(T_6\) of \(f(x) = x^4\) at \(x_0 = 1\) is \(1 + 4(x-1) + 12(x-1)^2 + 24(x-1)^3 + 24(x-1)^4\)."

(e) "A Taylor polynomial of degree \(n\) reproduces every polynomial of degree at most \(n\) exactly, at every \(x\)."

(f) "The Maclaurin series of every smooth function converges to that function for every \(x\)."

(g) "\(\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(x)\, g'(x)\)."

(h) "\(\frac{d}{dx}(2x + 1)^4 = 4(2x + 1)^3\)."

Hint

Write out the definition of \(T_n\) and check where the \(k!\) goes. For (b), try \(f(x) = \lvert x \rvert\) at 0; for (f), think of \(\log(1 + x)\) at \(x = 3\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. Learning is optimisation over the parameters (slide 205); the data are fixed numbers in the objective.

(b) False. The limit must exist as \(h \to 0\) from both sides. For \(\lvert x \rvert\) at 0 the one-sided limit from above is 1, from below it is \(-1\), so the derivative does not exist. (Slide 206 writes "for \(h > 0\)"; read it as the two-sided limit.)

(c) True. \(f(x_0 - \varepsilon) \approx f(x_0) - \varepsilon f'(x_0) > f(x_0)\) for small \(\varepsilon > 0\). In one dimension, "the derivative points in the direction of steepest ascent" (slide 206) means its sign tells you which way is uphill.

(d) False. This is the slide 211 slip: the coefficients must be \(f^{(k)}(1)/k!\), giving

\[ T_6(x) = 1 + 4(x-1) + 6(x-1)^2 + 4(x-1)^3 + (x-1)^4 = x^4. \]

The printed version gives 65 at \(x = 2\) instead of \(2^4 = 16\).

(e) True. All derivatives of order above the degree vanish, so the remainder is zero (slide 210).

(f) False. The Maclaurin series of \(\log(1 + x)\) diverges for \(\lvert x \rvert > 1\), and \(e^{-1/x^2}\) (with value 0 at 0) has every derivative 0 at 0, so its series is identically 0 although the function is not.

(g) False. The outer derivative is evaluated at the inner function: \(\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))\, g'(x)\). For \(\sin(x^2)\) the correct answer is \(2x\cos(x^2)\), not \(2x\cos x\).

(h) False. The inner derivative 2 is missing: \(\frac{d}{dx}(2x+1)^4 = 4(2x+1)^3 \cdot 2 = 8(2x+1)^3\) (slide 215).

Key insight: Most univariate mistakes are bookkeeping, not ideas: a missing \(k!\), a missing inner derivative, or an outer derivative evaluated at the wrong point.

P6.2 L2 · Computation

From the limit definition to a Taylor polynomial

(a) Use the limit definition and the binomial theorem to show that \(\frac{d}{dx} x^3 = 3x^2\).

(b) Use the limit definition to find the derivative of \(f(x) = \frac{1}{x}\) at \(x = 2\).

(c) For \(f(x) = x^3 - 2x\), compute \(T_2\) and \(T_3\) at \(x_0 = 2\).

(d) Evaluate \(T_2(3)\), \(T_3(3)\) and \(f(3)\). Which Taylor polynomial is exact, and why?

Hint

\((x + h)^3 = x^3 + 3x^2 h + 3x h^2 + h^3\). For (c) you need \(f(2)\), \(f'(2)\), \(f''(2)\), \(f'''(2)\), each divided by \(k!\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ \frac{(x+h)^3 - x^3}{h} = \frac{3x^2 h + 3x h^2 + h^3}{h} = 3x^2 + 3xh + h^2 \xrightarrow{h \to 0} \mathbf{3x^2}. \]

Only the \(i = 1\) term of the binomial sum survives; every term with \(i \ge 2\) still carries a factor of \(h\) (slides 207–208).

(b)

\[ \frac{\frac{1}{2+h} - \frac{1}{2}}{h} = \frac{2 - (2 + h)}{2(2+h)h} = \frac{-1}{2(2+h)} \xrightarrow{h \to 0} \mathbf{-\tfrac{1}{4}}, \]

which matches \(-1/x^2\) at \(x = 2\).

(c) \(f(2) = 4\), \(f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2\) so \(f'(2) = 10\), \(f''(x) = 6x\) so \(f''(2) = 12\), and \(f'''(x) = 6\). Dividing by \(k!\):

\[ T_2(x) = 4 + 10(x-2) + 6(x-2)^2, \qquad T_3(x) = 4 + 10(x-2) + 6(x-2)^2 + (x-2)^3. \]

(d) \(T_2(3) = 20\), \(T_3(3) = 21\), \(f(3) = 27 - 6 = 21\). \(T_3\) is exact (expanding it gives back \(x^3 - 2x\)) because \(f\) is a cubic, so every derivative of order 4 and above is zero. \(T_2\) misses by exactly the dropped term \((3 - 2)^3 = 1\).

Key insight: The limit definition is where \(nx^{n-1}\) comes from, and dividing the \(k\)-th derivative by \(k!\) is what makes a Taylor polynomial reproduce a polynomial exactly.

P6.3 L2 · Computation

Product, quotient and chain rules

Differentiate each function, simplify, and evaluate at the given points.

(a) \(h(x) = (3x^2 - 1)^5\), at \(x = 1\).

(b) \(p(x) = x^2 e^{-x}\), at \(x = 1\) and \(x = 2\).

(c) \(q(x) = \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\), at \(x = 0\), \(1\), \(2\).

(d) \(r(x) = \log(1 + e^{x})\) (the "softplus" activation), at \(x = 0\). Name the function you get.

Hint

(a) is a chain rule with inner \(3x^2 - 1\); (b) a product rule; (c) a quotient rule; (d) a chain rule with outer \(\log u\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Chain rule with \(u = 3x^2 - 1\), \(u' = 6x\):

\[ h'(x) = 5(3x^2 - 1)^4 \cdot 6x = 30x(3x^2 - 1)^4, \qquad h'(1) = 30 \cdot 2^4 = \mathbf{480}. \]

(b) Product rule:

\[ p'(x) = 2x e^{-x} - x^2 e^{-x} = x(2 - x)e^{-x}, \qquad p'(1) = \mathbf{e^{-1} \approx 0.3679}, \quad p'(2) = \mathbf{0}. \]

So \(x = 2\) is a stationary point of \(p\) (its maximum on \(x > 0\)).

(c) Quotient rule:

\[ q'(x) = \frac{(1)(1 + x^2) - x(2x)}{(1 + x^2)^2} = \frac{1 - x^2}{(1 + x^2)^2}, \qquad q'(0) = \mathbf{1}, \quad q'(1) = \mathbf{0}, \quad q'(2) = \mathbf{-\tfrac{3}{25}}. \]

(d) Chain rule with \(u = 1 + e^x\):

\[ r'(x) = \frac{e^x}{1 + e^x} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} = \sigma(x), \qquad r'(0) = \mathbf{\tfrac{1}{2}}. \]

The derivative of softplus is the sigmoid.

Key insight: Each rule handles one way of building a function (multiplying, dividing, nesting); identify the outermost operation first and the rule follows.

P6.4 L3 · Application

Fixing slide 211 and a Maclaurin expansion of \(e^x \cos x\)

(a) Compute \(f^{(k)}(1)\) for \(f(x) = x^4\) and \(k = 0, \dots, 6\), and write the Taylor polynomial \(T_6\) at \(x_0 = 1\). Expand it and confirm that it equals \(x^4\).

(b) Slide 211 prints \(T_6(x) = 1 + 4(x-1) + 12(x-1)^2 + 24(x-1)^3 + 24(x-1)^4\). Find the polynomial by which this differs from \(x^4\), and evaluate the slide's version at \(x = 2\).

(c) For \(g(x) = e^x \cos x\), compute \(g^{(k)}(0)\) for \(k = 0, \dots, 4\) and write the Maclaurin polynomial \(T_4\).

(d) Use \(T_4\) to approximate \(g(0.1)\) and compare with the true value.

(e) Show that \(g^{(4)}(x) = -4 g(x)\), and use this to predict \(g^{(5)}(0), \dots, g^{(8)}(0)\) without differentiating again.

Hint

For (c), \(\frac{d}{dx}\big(e^x(\alpha\cos x + \beta \sin x)\big) = e^x\big((\alpha + \beta)\cos x + (\beta - \alpha)\sin x\big)\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(f(1) = 1\), \(f'(1) = 4\), \(f''(1) = 12\), \(f'''(1) = 24\), \(f^{(4)}(1) = 24\), \(f^{(5)}(1) = f^{(6)}(1) = 0\). Dividing by \(0!, 1!, 2!, 3!, 4!\):

\[ T_6(x) = 1 + 4(x-1) + 6(x-1)^2 + 4(x-1)^3 + (x-1)^4 = \mathbf{x^4}. \]

The coefficients \(1, 4, 6, 4, 1\) are the binomial coefficients of \(\big((x - 1) + 1\big)^4\).

(b) Expanding the slide's polynomial and subtracting \(x^4\) gives

\[ \mathbf{23x^4 - 72x^3 + 84x^2 - 44x + 9}, \]

and the slide's version gives 65 at \(x = 2\) (\(1 + 4 + 12 + 24 + 24\)) instead of 16. The derivatives on the slide are right; the division by \(k!\) was forgotten.

(c) Applying the hint repeatedly:

\[ \begin{aligned} g &= e^x \cos x, & g(0) &= 1, \\ g' &= e^x(\cos x - \sin x), & g'(0) &= 1, \\ g'' &= -2e^x \sin x, & g''(0) &= 0, \\ g''' &= -2e^x(\sin x + \cos x), & g'''(0) &= -2, \\ g^{(4)} &= -4e^x \cos x, & g^{(4)}(0) &= -4. \end{aligned} \]

\[ T_4(x) = 1 + x + 0 \cdot \frac{x^2}{2!} - \frac{2x^3}{3!} - \frac{4x^4}{4!} = \mathbf{1 + x - \frac{x^3}{3} - \frac{x^4}{6}}. \]

(d) \(T_4(0.1) = 1 + 0.1 - 0.000333\ldots - 0.0000166\ldots = \mathbf{1.0996500}\), while \(g(0.1) = e^{0.1}\cos 0.1 = \mathbf{1.0996497}\). The error is about \(-3.3 \times 10^{-7}\), which matches the next term of the series, \(-x^5/30\) at \(x = 0.1\).

(e) The fourth line of (c) already shows \(g^{(4)} = -4e^x\cos x = -4g\). Hence \(g^{(k+4)}(0) = -4\, g^{(k)}(0)\):

\[ g^{(5)}(0) = -4, \quad g^{(6)}(0) = 0, \quad g^{(7)}(0) = 8, \quad g^{(8)}(0) = 16, \]

so the series continues \(-\frac{x^5}{30} + \frac{x^7}{630} + \frac{x^8}{2520} + \cdots\) (\(-4/5! = -1/30\), \(8/7! = 1/630\), \(16/8! = 1/2520\)). This is the same kind of period-4 pattern as the slide 212 example \(\sin x + \cos x\), but with a factor \(-4\) each cycle.

Key insight: A Taylor coefficient is a derivative divided by a factorial; forgetting the factorial does not just lose accuracy, it produces a different function, which you can catch by evaluating at a single point.

P6.5 L4 · Analysis

Product and quotient rules from the chain rule

Assume only the sum rule, the chain rule, and the power rule \(\frac{d}{du}u^n = nu^{n-1}\) for \(n = 2\) and \(n = -1\).

(a) Using the identity \(fg = \frac{1}{4}\big[(f + g)^2 - (f - g)^2\big]\), derive the product rule \((fg)' = f'g + fg'\).

(b) Use the chain rule on \(u \mapsto u^{-1}\) to show \(\left(\frac{1}{g}\right)' = -\frac{g'}{g^2}\), and then derive the quotient rule from (a).

(c) Check your quotient rule on \(q(x) = \frac{x}{1 + x^2}\) from P6.3.

(d) A student claims "\((fg)' = f' g'\)". Give a one-line counterexample. Then say what breaks in the quotient rule at a point where \(g(x_0) = 0\).

Hint

For (a), apply the chain rule to \((f \pm g)^2\): the derivative is \(2(f \pm g)(f' \pm g')\). Expand and subtract.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) By the chain rule with outer function \(u^2\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \big((f+g)^2\big)' &= 2(f+g)(f'+g') = 2(ff' + fg' + gf' + gg'), \\ \big((f-g)^2\big)' &= 2(f-g)(f'-g') = 2(ff' - fg' - gf' + gg'). \end{aligned} \]

Subtracting and dividing by 4:

\[ (fg)' = \tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 2 \cdot 2(fg' + gf') = \mathbf{f'g + fg'}. \]

(b) With outer function \(u^{-1}\) (derivative \(-u^{-2}\)) and inner function \(g\):

\[ \left(\frac{1}{g}\right)' = -\frac{1}{g^2}\, g' . \]

Then by the product rule,

\[ \left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \left(f \cdot \frac{1}{g}\right)' = \frac{f'}{g} - \frac{f g'}{g^2} = \mathbf{\frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}}. \]

(c) \(f = x\), \(g = 1 + x^2\): \(q' = \frac{(1 + x^2) - x \cdot 2x}{(1 + x^2)^2} = \frac{1 - x^2}{(1 + x^2)^2}\), the same as P6.3(c).

(d) \(f = g = x\): \((x^2)' = 2x\), but \(f'g' = 1\). At a point with \(g(x_0) = 0\) the function \(f/g\) is not even defined there, and the step \(\left(\frac{1}{g}\right)' = -g'/g^2\) divides by zero; the rule holds only where \(g \ne 0\).

Key insight: The chain rule is the master rule: products and quotients are compositions with \(u^2\) and \(u^{-1}\), which is exactly why automatic differentiation only needs a chain rule plus a small table of elementary derivatives.

8.B Partial Derivatives & Gradients (6.2)

P6.6 L1 · Foundation

Partial derivatives and the row gradient: true or false

Use the deck's row-gradient convention. Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "For \(f : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\), the gradient \(\frac{df}{dx}\) is a \(3 \times 1\) matrix."

(b) "\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\) is an ordinary one-variable derivative: freeze \(x_2, \dots, x_n\) and take the limit in \(x_1\) alone."

(c) "A function of two variables \(x_1, x_2\) that returns a number is a map \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\)."

(d) "In the chain rule \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} g(f(x)) = \frac{\partial g}{\partial f}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\), the two factors may be multiplied in either order, as for scalars."

(e) "If both partial derivatives of \(f(x, y)\) exist at the origin, then \(f\) is continuous there."

(f) "The gradient of \(f(x, y) = (x + 2y^3)^2\) at \((1, 0)\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\)."

(g) "For scalar functions \(f, g : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\), \(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(fg) = g\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + f\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}\), and the result is \(1 \times n\)."

Hint

Track shapes: \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial f}\) is \(1 \times m\) when \(g\) is scalar and \(f \in \mathbb{R}^m\), and \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) is \(m \times n\). For (e), look at \(f(x, y) = \frac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}\) with \(f(0, 0) = 0\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) False. In the deck's convention (slide 218) it is the row \(\begin{bmatrix} \partial f/\partial x_1 & \partial f/\partial x_2 & \partial f/\partial x_3 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 3}\). Its transpose is the \(3 \times 1\) column gradient.

(b) True. That is the definition on slide 217.

(c) False. It is \(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\). Slide 221 prints "\(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\) of two variables"; the domain must be \(\mathbb{R}^2\).

(d) False. \((1 \times m)(m \times n)\) is defined and gives \(1 \times n\); the reverse order \((m \times n)(1 \times m)\) is not even defined unless \(n = 1\). Matrix multiplication is not commutative (slide 220).

(e) False. For \(f = \frac{xy}{x^2 + y^2}\), \(f(0, 0) = 0\): \(f(x, 0) = f(0, y) = 0\), so both partials at the origin are 0, yet \(f(t, t) = \frac{1}{2}\) for every \(t \ne 0\), so \(f\) is not continuous at the origin. Partials only probe the two axis directions.

(f) True. \(\partial f/\partial x = 2(x + 2y^3) = 2\) and \(\partial f/\partial y = 12y^2(x + 2y^3) = 0\) at \((1, 0)\) (slide 218's formulas).

(g) True. \(f\) and \(g\) are scalars, so each term is a scalar times a \(1 \times n\) row.

Key insight: A gradient is a shaped object, not just a list of partials; keep track of the shape and the order of every factor, and the multivariate rules become the scalar rules again.

P6.7 L2 · Computation

Partial derivatives, the limit definition and a finite-difference check

Give every gradient as a row vector.

(a) Find the gradient of \(f(x, y) = (2x - y^2)^3\) and evaluate it at \((1, 1)\).

(b) Find the gradient of \(g(x_1, x_2) = x_1^3 x_2 + x_1 x_2^2\) and evaluate it at \((1, 2)\).

(c) Compute \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_1}(1, 2)\) again, directly from the limit definition.

(d) Estimate \(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x_1}(1, 2)\) with the forward difference \(\frac{g(1 + h, 2) - g(1, 2)}{h}\) and the central difference \(\frac{g(1 + h, 2) - g(1 - h, 2)}{2h}\), both with \(h = 0.1\). Which is closer, and by how much?

(e) Find the gradient of \(k(x) = x_1 e^{x_2 x_3}\) at \(x = (2, 0, 5)\), and state its shape.

Hint

In (c), expand \(g(1 + h, 2) = 2(1 + h)^3 + 4(1 + h)\) and subtract \(g(1, 2) = 6\) before dividing by \(h\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Chain rule with inner \(2x - y^2\):

\[ \frac{df}{d(x, y)} = \begin{bmatrix} 6(2x - y^2)^2 & -6y(2x - y^2)^2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \text{at } (1, 1): \ \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 6 & -6 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

(b)

\[ \frac{dg}{dx} = \begin{bmatrix} 3x_1^2 x_2 + x_2^2 & x_1^3 + 2x_1 x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \text{at } (1, 2): \ \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 10 & 5 \end{bmatrix}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}. \]

(c)

\[ \frac{g(1+h, 2) - g(1, 2)}{h} = \frac{2(3h + 3h^2 + h^3) + 4h}{h} = 10 + 6h + 2h^2 \xrightarrow{h \to 0} \mathbf{10}. \]

(d) From (c), the forward difference equals \(10 + 6h + 2h^2 = \mathbf{10.62}\) at \(h = 0.1\). The central difference is the average of the forward quotients at \(+h\) and \(-h\), so the odd term \(6h\) cancels and it equals \(10 + 2h^2 = \mathbf{10.02}\). The central difference is 30 times closer (error 0.02 against 0.62), because its error is \(O(h^2)\) rather than \(O(h)\).

(e)

\[ \frac{dk}{dx} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{x_2 x_3} & x_1 x_3 e^{x_2 x_3} & x_1 x_2 e^{x_2 x_3} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \text{at } (2, 0, 5): \ \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 10 & 0 \end{bmatrix}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 3}. \]

Key insight: Each partial derivative is a one-variable limit, so the one-variable tools carry over directly, including the finite-difference check, where the central difference is the one worth using.

P6.8 L2 · Computation

The chain rule for \(f(x_1(t), x_2(t))\)

Let \(f(x_1, x_2) = x_1 x_2 + x_2^2\) with \(x_1 = \cos t\) and \(x_2 = \sin t\).

(a) State the correct domain and codomain of \(f\), and the shapes of \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) and \(\frac{\partial x}{\partial t}\). (Slide 221 states this setting with a typo; say what it is.)

(b) Compute \(\frac{df}{dt}\) with the chain rule as a (row)(column) product, and simplify.

(c) Check (b) by substituting first and differentiating \(f(t)\) directly.

(d) Evaluate \(\frac{df}{dt}\) at \(t = \pi/4\) both from the matrix product (with numbers) and from your simplified formula.

(e) Check (d) with a central difference, \(h = 0.01\).

Hint

\(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \begin{bmatrix} x_2 & x_1 + 2x_2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(\frac{\partial x}{\partial t} = \begin{bmatrix} -\sin t \\ \cos t \end{bmatrix}\). You will need \(\cos^2 t - \sin^2 t = \cos 2t\) and \(2 \sin t \cos t = \sin 2t\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) (slide 221 writes \(f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}\), which cannot take two inputs). \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}\) and \(\frac{\partial x}{\partial t} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 1}\), so the product is \(1 \times 1\).

(b)

\[ \frac{df}{dt} = \begin{bmatrix} x_2 & x_1 + 2x_2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -\sin t \\ \cos t \end{bmatrix} = -\sin^2 t + \cos^2 t + 2\sin t\cos t = \mathbf{\cos 2t + \sin 2t}. \]

(c) \(f(t) = \sin t \cos t + \sin^2 t = \tfrac{1}{2}\sin 2t + \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2t)\), so \(f'(t) = \cos 2t + \sin 2t\), the same.

(d) At \(t = \pi/4\), \(x_1 = x_2 = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\):

\[ \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \tfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} -\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \end{bmatrix} = -\tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{3}{2} = \mathbf{1}, \]

and \(\cos\frac{\pi}{2} + \sin\frac{\pi}{2} = 0 + 1 = 1\).

(e) \(\frac{f(\pi/4 + 0.01) - f(\pi/4 - 0.01)}{0.02} \approx \mathbf{0.99993}\), within \(7 \times 10^{-5}\) of 1. (The forward difference gives about 0.98993, an error 150 times larger.)

Key insight: The multivariate chain rule adds up one contribution per intermediate variable, \(\sum_i \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\frac{dx_i}{dt}\), and writing it as a row times a column makes that sum automatic.

P6.9 L3 · Application

\(f(g(s, t))\) with a vector-valued inner function

Let \(f(u_1, u_2) = u_1^2 + 3u_1 u_2\) and \(u = g(s, t) = \begin{bmatrix} st \\ s + t^2 \end{bmatrix}\). Use row gradients throughout and work at \((s, t) = (1, 2)\).

(a) Give the shapes of \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\), \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial (s, t)}\) and \(\frac{df}{d(s, t)}\).

(b) Compute \(u\), \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\) and \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial (s, t)}\) at the point, and then \(\frac{df}{d(s, t)}\) as a matrix product.

(c) Verify (b) by substituting \(u = g(s, t)\) into \(f\) and differentiating directly.

(d) A classmate computes \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial (s, t)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\). Explain why this fails, and show that \(\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial (s, t)}\right)^\top \left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial u}\right)^\top\) is the correct column-layout version.

(e) Use the product rule for \(p = u_1 u_2\) to find \(\frac{dp}{d(s, t)}\) at the same point, and check it by direct substitution.

Hint

\(\frac{\partial u}{\partial (s, t)} = \begin{bmatrix} t & s \\ 1 & 2t \end{bmatrix}\). Row \(i\) is the gradient of \(u_i\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(f : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}\) and \(g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2\), so \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial u} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}\), \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial (s, t)} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}\) and \(\frac{df}{d(s, t)} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}\).

(b) At \((1, 2)\): \(u = (2, 5)\).

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial u} = \begin{bmatrix} 2u_1 + 3u_2 & 3u_1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 6 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \frac{\partial u}{\partial (s, t)} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}, \]

\[ \frac{df}{d(s, t)} = \begin{bmatrix} 19 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 44 & 43 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

(c) \(f(s, t) = s^2t^2 + 3st(s + t^2) = s^2t^2 + 3s^2t + 3st^3\), so

\[ \frac{\partial f}{\partial s} = 2st^2 + 6st + 3t^3 = 8 + 12 + 24 = 44, \qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = 2s^2t + 3s^2 + 9st^2 = 4 + 3 + 36 = 43. \]

Central differences with \(h = 10^{-3}\) give 44.000 and 43.000 as well.

(d) \((2 \times 2)(1 \times 2)\) is not a defined product. In column layout every object is transposed and the order reverses, \((AB)^\top = B^\top A^\top\):

\[ \left(\frac{df}{d(s, t)}\right)^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix}^\top \begin{bmatrix} 19 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 38 + 6 \\ 19 + 24 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 44 \\ 43 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(Here the Jacobian is symmetric, so forgetting the transpose would go unnoticed; with a non-symmetric Jacobian it would give a wrong answer.)

(e) Product rule for two scalar functions of \((s, t)\):

\[ \frac{dp}{d(s, t)} = u_2 \frac{\partial u_1}{\partial (s, t)} + u_1 \frac{\partial u_2}{\partial (s, t)} = 5\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + 2\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 12 & 13 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Directly, \(p = s^2t + st^3\), so \(\partial p/\partial s = 2st + t^3 = 12\) and \(\partial p/\partial t = s^2 + 3st^2 = 13\).

Key insight: For \(f(g(x))\) with vector \(g\), the gradient is (row gradient of the outer function) times (Jacobian of the inner function); the layout you choose fixes the order, and the shapes tell you immediately whether you have it right.

8.C Gradients of Vector-valued Functions: Jacobians (6.3)

P6.10 L1 · Foundation

What shape is that derivative?

Use the deck's layout (row gradients, \(m \times n\) Jacobians). Give the shape of each derivative, or say true or false with a reason.

(a) \(\frac{df}{dx}\) for \(f : \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3\).

(b) \(\frac{d}{dx}(Ax)\) for \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{5 \times 2}\).

(c) \(\frac{dg}{dt}\) for a curve \(g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^3\).

(d) \(\frac{dL}{d\theta}\) for a training loss \(L : \mathbb{R}^{100} \to \mathbb{R}\).

(e) \(\frac{d}{dx} L(f(x))\) for \(f : \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) and \(L : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\), with the shapes of both factors.

(f) \(\frac{da}{dZ}\) for the element-wise sigmoid \(a = \sigma(Z)\), \(Z \in \mathbb{R}^m\). What is special about it?

(g) True or false: "Column \(j\) of the Jacobian of \(f\) is \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_j}\), the rate of change of the whole output vector as \(x_j\) alone moves."

(h) True or false: "\(\frac{d}{dx}(Ax) = A^\top\)."

(i) A layer maps \(x \in \mathbb{R}^{784}\) to \(z = Wx \in \mathbb{R}^{128}\). What is the shape of \(\frac{dz}{dx}\)? How many numbers does \(\frac{dz}{dW}\) contain?

Hint

Jacobian shape is (output dimension) \(\times\) (input dimension). A matrix of \(p\) entries counts as \(p\) inputs.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(3 \times 4\).

(b) \(5 \times 2\); it is \(A\) itself (slide 228).

(c) \(3 \times 1\), a column (the velocity of the curve).

(d) \(1 \times 100\), a row.

(e) \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial f} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 3}\) times \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 4}\) gives \(1 \times 4\).

(f) \(m \times m\), and diagonal, \(\operatorname{diag}\big(a \odot (1 - a)\big)\), because \(a_i\) depends only on \(Z_i\) (slides 250–252).

(g) True. That is how slide 227 builds the Jacobian: the partial derivative of a vector-valued function is itself a column.

(h) False in this layout: \(\partial(Ax)_i / \partial x_j = A_{ij}\), so the Jacobian is \(A\). (\(A^\top\) appears in the column layout of the gradient of a scalar, for example \(\partial \text{Loss}/\partial x = A^\top \delta^{(Z)}\) on slide 255.)

(i) \(\frac{dz}{dx} = W\), shape \(128 \times 784\). \(\frac{dz}{dW}\) has one entry \(\partial z_i / \partial W_{jk}\) for each output and each weight: \(128 \times 128 \times 784 = \mathbf{12{,}845{,}056}\) numbers, almost all zero (\(\partial z_i / \partial W_{jk} = 0\) unless \(i = j\)). This is why backpropagation never forms such tensors and works with \(\partial \text{Loss}/\partial W\), which has the shape of \(W\).

Key insight: Shape first: (outputs) \(\times\) (inputs) tells you what a derivative is before you compute a single entry, and it catches most chain-rule errors for free.

P6.11 L2 · Computation

Computing Jacobians and using them to linearise

(a) Find the Jacobian of

\[ f(x_1, x_2) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1^2 x_2 \\ 5x_1 + \sin x_2 \\ x_2 e^{x_1} \end{bmatrix} \]

and evaluate it at \(x_0 = (1, 0)\). State its shape.

(b) Use the linearisation \(f(x_0 + \Delta) \approx f(x_0) + J\Delta\) with \(\Delta = (0.1, -0.1)\) to estimate \(f(1.1, -0.1)\), and compare with the true value.

(c) For \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), write \(f(x) = Ax\) component by component, compute every partial derivative, and confirm that \(\frac{df}{dx} = A\).

(d) Why is the linearisation of \(f(x) = Ax\) exact for every \(\Delta\)?

Hint

Row \(i\) of the Jacobian is the gradient of \(f_i\). For (b), \(f(x_0) = (0, 5, 0)\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ J = \begin{bmatrix} 2x_1 x_2 & x_1^2 \\ 5 & \cos x_2 \\ x_2 e^{x_1} & e^{x_1} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad J(1, 0) = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 5 & 1 \\ 0 & e \end{bmatrix}} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}. \]

(b)

\[ f(x_0) + J\Delta = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 5 & 1 \\ 0 & e \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 0.1 \\ -0.1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0.1 \\ 5.4 \\ -0.1e \end{bmatrix} \approx \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} -0.1000 \\ 5.4000 \\ -0.2718 \end{bmatrix}}, \]

while the true value is \(f(1.1, -0.1) = (-0.121,\ 5.40017,\ -0.30042)\). The errors (about 0.02, 0.0002 and 0.03) are second order in \(\lVert \Delta \rVert\).

(c) \(f_1 = x_1 + 2x_2\) and \(f_2 = -x_1 + 3x_2 + 4x_3\), so

\[ \frac{df}{dx} = \begin{bmatrix} \partial f_1/\partial x_1 & \partial f_1/\partial x_2 & \partial f_1/\partial x_3 \\ \partial f_2/\partial x_1 & \partial f_2/\partial x_2 & \partial f_2/\partial x_3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}. \]

In general \(f_i = \sum_j A_{ij}x_j\) gives \(\partial f_i / \partial x_j = A_{ij}\) (slide 228).

(d) \(f(x_0 + \Delta) = Ax_0 + A\Delta = f(x_0) + J\Delta\) exactly: a linear map is its own linearisation, and all second derivatives are zero.

Key insight: The Jacobian is the best linear approximation of a vector-valued map near a point, and for a linear map \(Ax\) it is simply \(A\).

P6.12 L3 · Application

Shape-checked chain rules, scalar and vector

(a) Let \(h(t) = f(g(t))\) with \(f(x) = x_1 e^{x_2}\) and \(g(t) = \begin{bmatrix} t^2 \\ 1 - t \end{bmatrix}\). Give the shapes of \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) and \(\frac{dg}{dt}\), compute \(h'(1)\) with the chain rule, and check it by differentiating \(h(t) = t^2 e^{1 - t}\) directly.

(b) Now let \(g : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3\) and \(F : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2\) be

\[ g(x) = \begin{bmatrix} x_1 + x_2 \\ x_1 x_2 \\ x_2^2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad F(u) = \begin{bmatrix} u_1 u_2 \\ u_2 + u_3^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

At \(x = (1, 2)\), compute \(u = g(x)\), \(J_g\), \(J_F\) (at \(u\)), and the Jacobian of \(F \circ g\) as a product. State every shape.

(c) Verify (b) by writing out \(F(g(x))\) and differentiating directly.

(d) The product \(J_g J_F\) is also defined. What is its shape, and why is it not the Jacobian of \(F \circ g\)?

(e) Add a scalar loss \(L(v) = \frac{1}{2}\lVert v \rVert^2\) on top, with \(v = F(g(x))\). Compute \(\frac{dL}{dx}\) at \(x = (1, 2)\) by multiplying from the left: first \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} J_F\), then that row times \(J_g\).

Hint

\(J_g = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ x_2 & x_1 \\ 0 & 2x_2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(J_F = \begin{bmatrix} u_2 & u_1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2u_3 \end{bmatrix}\). For (e), \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} = v^\top\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{x_2} & x_1 e^{x_2} \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}\) and \(\frac{dg}{dt} = \begin{bmatrix} 2t \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 1}\), so \((1 \times 2)(2 \times 1) = 1 \times 1\). At \(t = 1\), \(x = (1, 0)\):

\[ h'(1) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{1}. \]

Directly, \(h'(t) = (2t - t^2)e^{1 - t}\), which is \(1\) at \(t = 1\).

(b) \(u = g(1, 2) = (3, 2, 4)\).

\[ J_F J_g = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 8 \end{bmatrix}}_{2 \times 3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}}_{3 \times 2} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ 2 & 33 \end{bmatrix}} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}. \]

(c) \(F(g(x)) = \begin{bmatrix} (x_1 + x_2)x_1x_2 \\ x_1x_2 + x_2^4 \end{bmatrix}\). Its partials are

\[ \begin{bmatrix} x_1x_2 + (x_1 + x_2)x_2 & x_1x_2 + (x_1 + x_2)x_1 \\ x_2 & x_1 + 4x_2^3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 6 & 2 + 3 \\ 2 & 1 + 32 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ 2 & 33 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(d) \(J_g J_F\) is \((3 \times 2)(2 \times 3) = 3 \times 3\). A composition \(\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2\) must have a \(2 \times 2\) Jacobian, so the shape alone rules it out. (A \(3 \times 3\) product of this kind would belong to \(g \circ F\), a map \(\mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3\), and even then the factors would have to be evaluated at different points.) A defined product is not automatically the right product.

(e) \(v = F(u) = (6, 18)\), so \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial v} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 18 \end{bmatrix}\).

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 18 \end{bmatrix} J_F = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 36 & 144 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \begin{bmatrix} 12 & 36 & 144 \end{bmatrix} J_g = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 84 & 624 \end{bmatrix}}, \]

which agrees with \(\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 18 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ 2 & 33 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 48 + 36 & 30 + 594 \end{bmatrix}\). Multiplying from the left keeps every intermediate result a single row, so no Jacobian-times-Jacobian product is ever formed; that is the idea behind backpropagation (8.E–8.F).

Key insight: The Jacobian of a composition is the product of the Jacobians in the order of the composition, each evaluated at its own input; when a scalar loss sits on top, multiplying from the left turns that product into a sequence of cheap row-times-matrix steps.

8.D Matrix-calculus Identities (6.4)

P6.13 L1 · Foundation

The identities of slide 235: true or false

Row layout for derivatives with respect to a vector, same-shape-as-\(X\) layout for derivatives with respect to a matrix. Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "\(\frac{\partial (a^\top x)}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial (x^\top a)}{\partial x} = a^\top\)."

(b) "\(\frac{\partial (x^\top B x)}{\partial x} = 2x^\top B\) for every square matrix \(B\)."

(c) "For \(a \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(b \in \mathbb{R}^n\), \(\frac{\partial (a^\top X b)}{\partial X} = ab^\top\), which has the same shape as \(X\)."

(d) "For \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}\) and \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), \(\frac{\partial\, \operatorname{tr}(AX)}{\partial X} = A\)."

(e) "\(\frac{\partial}{\partial s}(x - As)^\top W (x - As) = -2(x - As)^\top W A\) for every square \(W\)."

(f) "\(\frac{\partial \lVert x \rVert^2}{\partial x} = 2x^\top\), and \(\frac{\partial \lVert x \rVert}{\partial x} = \frac{x^\top}{\lVert x \rVert}\) for \(x \ne 0\)."

Hint

Test each claim on the smallest example that could break it: a non-symmetric \(2 \times 2\) matrix such as \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), for which \(x^\top B x = x_1 x_2\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. \(a^\top x = x^\top a = \sum_i a_i x_i\), and \(\partial/\partial x_i = a_i\).

(b) False. The general identity is \(x^\top(B + B^\top)\). For \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(x^\top B x = x_1x_2\) has gradient \(\begin{bmatrix} x_2 & x_1 \end{bmatrix}\), while \(2x^\top B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2x_1 \end{bmatrix}\). The shortcut \(2x^\top B\) is right only for symmetric \(B\).

(c) True. \(a^\top X b = \sum_{i,j} a_i X_{ij} b_j\), so \(\partial / \partial X_{ij} = a_i b_j\), the \((i, j)\) entry of the \(m \times n\) matrix \(ab^\top\).

(d) False. \(\operatorname{tr}(AX) = \sum_{i,j} A_{ji} X_{ij}\), so \(\partial / \partial X_{ij} = A_{ji}\): the derivative is \(A^\top\), which (unlike \(A\)) has the shape \(m \times n\) of \(X\).

(e) False. Slide 235 adds "for symmetric \(W\)" for a reason. In general the derivative is \(-(x - As)^\top(W + W^\top)A\), which reduces to \(-2(x - As)^\top WA\) only when \(W = W^\top\).

(f) True. \(\lVert x \rVert^2 = x^\top x\) is (b) with \(B = I\). For the norm, the chain rule with \(\sqrt{u}\) gives \(\frac{1}{2\lVert x \rVert} \cdot 2x^\top\); the norm is not differentiable at \(x = 0\).

Key insight: The quadratic-form identities hide a symmetrisation, \(B + B^\top\); forgetting it is harmless for covariance and Hessian matrices but wrong for a general weight matrix.

P6.14 L2 · Computation

Two vector identities, checked numerically

Let

\[ a = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(a) Compute \(a^\top x\) and its gradient with respect to \(x\) (row layout).

(b) Compute \(x^\top B x\) and its gradient \(x^\top(B + B^\top)\).

(c) Compute the two common wrong answers \(2x^\top B\) and \((2Bx)^\top\), and compare.

(d) A central-difference check with \(h = 10^{-4}\) on \(x^\top B x\) returns \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 13 & 8 \end{bmatrix}\), with error far below \(h^2\). Explain why the central difference is exact (apart from round-off) for this function.

Hint

\(Bx = (5, 5, 5)\) and \(x^\top B = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 8 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). The gradient is their sum.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(a^\top x = 2 - 2 - 3 = -3\), gradient \(a^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\) (independent of \(x\)).

(b) \(x^\top B x = x^\top(Bx) = 5 + 10 - 5 = 10\).

\[ B + B^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 6 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x^\top(B + B^\top) = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 13 & 8 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Equivalently \(x^\top B + (Bx)^\top = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 8 & 3 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 5 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\).

(c) \(2x^\top B = \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 16 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) and \((2Bx)^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 10 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\). Both are wrong, and the correct gradient is their average: each uses only one of the two places where \(x\) appears.

(d) For a quadratic \(q\), the Taylor expansion along \(e_i\) stops at second order:

\[ q(x \pm he_i) = q(x) \pm h\,\frac{\partial q}{\partial x_i} + \frac{h^2}{2}\frac{\partial^2 q}{\partial x_i^2}, \]

so \(\frac{q(x + he_i) - q(x - he_i)}{2h} = \frac{\partial q}{\partial x_i}\) exactly. The \(O(h^2)\) error term of the central difference involves the third derivative, which is zero here.

Key insight: \(x\) appears twice in \(x^\top B x\), so the product rule produces two terms, \(x^\top B\) and \(x^\top B^\top\); a quick finite-difference check exposes either one-term shortcut immediately.

P6.15 L3 · Application

The least-squares and weighted least-squares gradients

Let

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(a) Derive \(\frac{d}{dx}\lVert Ax - b \rVert^2 = 2(Ax - b)^\top A\) (row layout) with the chain rule through \(r = Ax - b\).

(b) Evaluate \(\lVert Ax - b \rVert^2\) and its gradient at the given \(x\). Check with central differences.

(c) Slide 235 gives \(\frac{\partial}{\partial s}(x - As)^\top W(x - As) = -2(x - As)^\top WA\) for symmetric \(W\). With the same \(A\), \(x_{\text{obs}} = (1, 0, 2)\), \(s = (1, 1)\) and

\[ W = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

evaluate the weighted loss and its gradient with respect to \(s\). (Here \(x_{\text{obs}}\) plays the role of the slide's \(x\).)

(d) Repeat the gradient computation for the non-symmetric \(W' = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), once with the slide's formula and once with the general formula \(-(x_{\text{obs}} - As)^\top(W' + W'^\top)A\). Which one does a finite-difference check agree with?

Hint

For (a): \(\frac{d}{dr}(r^\top r) = 2r^\top\) (1 \(\times\) 3) and \(\frac{dr}{dx} = A\) (3 \(\times\) 2). For (c), put \(q = x_{\text{obs}} - As\); then \(\frac{dq}{ds} = -A\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(L = r^\top r\) with \(r = Ax - b\). By the chain rule,

\[ \frac{dL}{dx} = \underbrace{\frac{dL}{dr}}_{1 \times 3}\underbrace{\frac{dr}{dx}}_{3 \times 2} = 2r^\top A = 2(Ax - b)^\top A \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times 2}. \]

(b) \(Ax = (-1, -1, -1)\), so \(r = (-2, -3, -4)\) and

\[ \lVert Ax - b \rVert^2 = 4 + 9 + 16 = \mathbf{29}, \qquad 2r^\top A = 2\begin{bmatrix} -2 - 9 + 0 & -4 - 12 - 4 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} -22 & -40 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Central differences give \(\begin{bmatrix} -22 & -40 \end{bmatrix}\) (exactly, since the loss is quadratic).

(c) \(As = (3, 7, 1)\), \(q = x_{\text{obs}} - As = (-2, -7, 1)\) and \(Wq = (-11, -23, 1)\):

\[ q^\top W q = 22 + 161 + 1 = \mathbf{184}, \qquad -2q^\top W A = -2(Wq)^\top A = -2\begin{bmatrix} -80 & -113 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 160 & 226 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Central differences agree.

(d) The slide's formula gives \(-2q^\top W'A = \begin{bmatrix} 24 & 32 \end{bmatrix}\); the general formula gives \(\begin{bmatrix} 26 & 44 \end{bmatrix}\), and the finite-difference check agrees with the general formula. Since \(q^\top W' q = q^\top \tfrac{1}{2}(W' + W'^\top) q\), only the symmetric part of \(W\) matters in the loss, and the slide's identity is correct once \(W\) has been symmetrised.

Key insight: Every least-squares gradient is "2 × residual\(^\top\) × weight × Jacobian of the residual"; the symmetry condition on \(W\) is not decoration, it is the \(B + B^\top\) of P6.13 in disguise.

P6.16 L3 · Application

Derivatives with respect to a matrix: trace, bilinear form and Frobenius norm

Derivatives with respect to a matrix \(X\) are written with the same shape as \(X\). Let

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}, \qquad X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}, \qquad a = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad b = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(a) Compute \(\operatorname{tr}(AX)\). Write \(\operatorname{tr}(AX)\) as a double sum, find \(\partial\, \operatorname{tr}(AX) / \partial X_{ij}\), and hence \(\frac{\partial\, \operatorname{tr}(AX)}{\partial X}\) for these matrices.

(b) Check one entry: increase \(X_{13}\) (row 1, column 3) by \(\varepsilon\) and find the change in \(\operatorname{tr}(AX)\).

(c) Compute \(a^\top X b\) and \(\frac{\partial (a^\top X b)}{\partial X} = ab^\top\).

(d) Show that \(a^\top X b = \operatorname{tr}(ba^\top X)\), and use (a) to rederive \(ab^\top\).

(e) Find \(\frac{\partial}{\partial X}\lVert X \rVert_F^2\), where \(\lVert X \rVert_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(X^\top X) = \sum_{i,j} X_{ij}^2\), and evaluate it at the given \(X\).

Hint

\(\operatorname{tr}(AX) = \sum_k (AX)_{kk} = \sum_k \sum_i A_{ki} X_{ik}\). For (d), use \(\operatorname{tr}(uv^\top M) = v^\top M u\), a consequence of the cyclic property of the trace.

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ AX = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 6 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \operatorname{tr}(AX) = -1 - 1 + 6 = \mathbf{4}. \]

\(\operatorname{tr}(AX) = \sum_{k}\sum_{i} A_{ki}X_{ik}\), and \(X_{ij}\) appears once, with coefficient \(A_{ji}\). So

\[ \frac{\partial\, \operatorname{tr}(AX)}{\partial X} = A^\top = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}, \]

the same shape as \(X\). (Central differences on all six entries return this matrix.)

(b) The \((1, 3)\) entry of \(A^\top\) is \(A_{31} = 3\), so the trace increases by \(3\varepsilon\). Directly: \(X_{13}\) only affects column 3 of \(AX\), whose diagonal entry is \((AX)_{33} = A_{31}X_{13} + A_{32}X_{23}\); its coefficient on \(X_{13}\) is 3.

(c) \(Xb = (5, -3)\), so \(a^\top X b = 5 + 6 = \mathbf{11}\), and

\[ \frac{\partial (a^\top X b)}{\partial X} = ab^\top = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 & 1 \\ -6 & 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Central differences agree. The middle column is zero because \(b_2 = 0\): column 2 of \(X\) never enters \(Xb\).

(d) \(a^\top X b\) is a scalar, so it equals its own trace, and the trace is cyclic:

\[ a^\top X b = \operatorname{tr}(a^\top X b) = \operatorname{tr}(b a^\top X). \]

This is \(\operatorname{tr}(MX)\) with \(M = ba^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2}\), so by (a) the derivative is \(M^\top = (ba^\top)^\top = ab^\top\).

(e) \(\partial / \partial X_{ij} \sum X_{kl}^2 = 2X_{ij}\), so

\[ \frac{\partial \lVert X \rVert_F^2}{\partial X} = 2X = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}, \]

the matrix analogue of \(\frac{d}{dx}\lVert x \rVert^2 = 2x^\top\). It is the gradient of the weight-decay penalty \(\lambda \lVert W \rVert_F^2\) used in training.

Key insight: For a scalar function of a matrix, write it as a sum over entries, read off the coefficient of \(X_{ij}\), and arrange the answers in the shape of \(X\); the trace identities are shortcuts for that bookkeeping.

P6.17 L4 · Analysis

Deriving the normal equations

A linear model \(\hat{y} = Xw\) is fitted by minimising \(L(w) = \lVert Xw - y \rVert^2\), where \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times D}\) has the training inputs as rows.

(a) Derive \(\frac{dL}{dw} = 2(Xw - y)^\top X\) (row layout) in two ways: from the chain rule through \(r = Xw - y\), and by expanding \(L\) into \(w^\top X^\top X w - 2y^\top X w + y^\top y\) and applying the identities of slide 235.

(b) Set the gradient to zero and obtain the normal equations \(X^\top X w = X^\top y\).

(c) Fit \(y = w_0 + w_1 t\) to the four points \((t, y) = (0, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (3, 5)\). Give \(w\) exactly, the residuals, \(L(w)\), and confirm that the gradient is zero.

(d) Show that the critical point is a minimum, and compute the eigenvalues of the Hessian \(2X^\top X\) for (c).

(e) What breaks if a third column \(2t\) is added to \(X\)? Describe the set of minimisers.

Hint

\(y^\top X w\) is a scalar of the form \(a^\top w\) with \(a = X^\top y\), and \(w^\top (X^\top X) w\) is a quadratic form with a symmetric matrix.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Chain rule. \(\frac{dL}{dr} = 2r^\top\) (\(1 \times N\)) and \(\frac{dr}{dw} = X\) (\(N \times D\)), so \(\frac{dL}{dw} = 2(Xw - y)^\top X \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times D}\).

Identities. \(L = w^\top X^\top X w - 2y^\top X w + y^\top y\). With \(B = X^\top X\) symmetric, \(\frac{\partial}{\partial w}(w^\top B w) = w^\top(B + B^\top) = 2w^\top X^\top X\), and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial w}(y^\top X w) = y^\top X\). Hence

\[ \frac{dL}{dw} = 2w^\top X^\top X - 2y^\top X = 2(Xw - y)^\top X. \]

(b) Setting it to zero and transposing:

\[ 2(Xw - y)^\top X = 0 \iff X^\top(Xw - y) = 0 \iff \mathbf{X^\top X w = X^\top y}. \]

The residual is orthogonal to every column of \(X\).

(c)

\[ X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad X^\top X = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & 14 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad X^\top y = \begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ 22 \end{bmatrix}. \]

\[ w = \frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 14 & -6 \\ -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 11 \\ 22 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix} 22 \\ 22 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 11/10 \\ 11/10 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

Predictions \(1.1, 2.2, 3.3, 4.4\), residuals \(Xw - y = (0.1, -0.8, 1.3, -0.6)\), and \(L(w) = 0.01 + 0.64 + 1.69 + 0.36 = 2.7\). The gradient \(2(Xw - y)^\top X = 2\begin{bmatrix} 0.1 - 0.8 + 1.3 - 0.6 & -0.8 + 2.6 - 1.8 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). (At \(w = 0\), by contrast, the gradient is \(\begin{bmatrix} -22 & -44 \end{bmatrix}\), and a gradient-descent step moves along \(-(\nabla L)^\top = (22, 44)\).)

(d) \(L\) is a quadratic with Hessian \(2X^\top X\), and \(v^\top X^\top X v = \lVert Xv \rVert^2 \ge 0\), so \(L\) is convex and every critical point is a global minimum. Here

\[ 2X^\top X = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 12 \\ 12 & 28 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \lambda = 18 \pm 2\sqrt{61} \approx \mathbf{2.380 \text{ and } 33.620}, \]

both positive, so the minimum is unique.

(e) The columns become dependent (\(\text{col}_3 = 2\,\text{col}_2\)), so \(X^\top X\) is singular and cannot be inverted. The normal equations still have solutions, but infinitely many: every \(w = (1.1,\ 1.1 - 2c,\ c)\) gives the same predictions and the same minimum \(L = 2.7\). The minimisers form a line in the direction \((0, -2, 1)\), the null space of \(X\). Regularisation (\(+\lambda\lVert w \rVert^2\)) or the pseudo-inverse picks one of them.

Key insight: "Gradient equals zero" turns least squares into a linear system; the identities of slide 235 do the calculus, and linear algebra (rank of \(X\)) decides whether the answer is unique.

P6.18 L5 · Mastery

Row or column? A layout trap in a gradient-descent step

Three sources give the gradient of \(f(x) = x^\top B x - a^\top x\):

  • Source R (the MFML deck, slides 218 and 235): \(\frac{df}{dx} = x^\top(B + B^\top) - a^\top\).
  • Source C (a column-layout textbook): \(\nabla f = (B + B^\top)x - a\).
  • Source S (a cheat sheet): \(\nabla f = 2Bx - a\).

Take \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(a = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(x_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\) and step size \(\gamma = 0.1\).

(a) A student says "Sources R and C disagree, because the gradient is a column vector in every textbook." Assess this.

(b) Compute one gradient-descent step from \(x_0\) using Source R correctly, and give \(f(x_0)\) and \(f(x_1)\).

(c) In NumPy, the student stores \(x_0\) as a \(2 \times 1\) array and the gradient from Source R as a \(1 \times 2\) array, then writes x - 0.1 * g. What comes out, and why does the code not crash?

(d) Find the true minimiser of \(f\). Then find where gradient descent with Source S's formula converges, and the true gradient there.

(e) State a rule that makes your own code immune to all three traps.

Hint

\(B + B^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Gradient descent with a formula \(g(x)\) stops where \(g(x) = 0\), whether or not \(g\) is the real gradient.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The claim is false. Sources R and C contain the same numbers; one is the transpose of the other. Layout is a convention: the deck (following Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong) uses the row ("numerator") layout so that the chain rule is a left-to-right product of Jacobians, while many ML texts use the column ("denominator") layout so that the gradient has the shape of \(x\). Neither is wrong; mixing them is. The deck itself switches to column layout on slides 254–255. Source S is the one that is actually wrong, because \(B\) is not symmetric.

(b) \(x_0^\top(B + B^\top) - a^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). The update needs a column, so transpose:

\[ x_1 = x_0 - \gamma\left(\frac{df}{dx}\right)^\top = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - 0.1\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{\begin{bmatrix} 0.6 \\ 0.9 \end{bmatrix}}. \]

\(f(x_0) = 4 - 3 = \mathbf{1}\) and \(f(x_1) = 2.07 - 2.4 = \mathbf{-0.33}\), a decrease.

(c) Broadcasting turns \((2 \times 1) - (1 \times 2)\) into a \(2 \times 2\) array,

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 0.6 & 0.9 \\ 0.6 & 0.9 \end{bmatrix}, \]

whose entries look plausible, so the bug can survive several iterations before shapes blow up elsewhere. No error is raised; the result is meaningless.

(d) The true minimiser solves \((B + B^\top)x = a\):

\[ \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \ \Rightarrow\ \mathbf{x^* = (0, 1)}, \qquad f(x^*) = \mathbf{-1}. \]

(\(B + B^\top\) has eigenvalues \(3 \pm \sqrt{2} > 0\), so this is the unique minimum.) Gradient descent with Source S stops where \(2Bx = a\), at \(x = (-\tfrac{1}{4}, 1)\), where \(f = -0.875\). The true gradient there is \(\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -\tfrac{1}{4} \end{bmatrix} \ne 0\). (With \(\gamma = 0.1\) both iterations do converge, to these two different points.) A wrong gradient does not announce itself; it just converges to the wrong answer.

(e) For example: (1) pick one layout and write it at the top of the code; (2) assert shapes (assert g.shape == x.shape) before every update; (3) never use a shortcut like \(2Bx\) without checking that \(B\) is symmetric; (4) run a central-difference gradient check on a random point before trusting any hand-derived gradient. Check (4) alone would have caught Source S at \(x_0\): it gives \((5, 0)\) against the true \((4, 1)\).

Key insight: Row versus column is a convention, not a correctness issue, but the update \(x - \gamma(\cdot)\) needs an object of the same shape as \(x\); write the transpose explicitly, assert shapes, and verify the formula numerically.

8.E Backpropagation (6.5)

P6.19 L2 · Computation

Expression swell, and how intermediate variables cure it

Let \(f(x) = \sqrt{x^2 + e^{x}} + \left(x^2 + e^{x}\right)^2\).

(a) Differentiate \(f\) symbolically, writing out every sub-expression in full (as slide 236 does for its example).

(b) Which sub-expressions repeat in \(f'(x)\)? How many times is \(e^x\) evaluated if \(f(x)\) and \(f'(x)\) are computed from the fully written-out formulas?

(c) Introduce \(u = x^2 + e^{x}\), \(v = \sqrt{u}\), \(w = u^2\), \(f = v + w\). Write \(f'(x)\) in terms of these, and evaluate \(f(0)\), \(f'(0)\), \(f(1)\) and \(f'(1)\).

(d) Check \(f'(1)\) with a central difference.

Hint

Both outer pieces depend on \(x\) only through \(u\), so \(f'(x) = \left(\frac{dv}{du} + \frac{dw}{du}\right)\frac{du}{dx}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a)

\[ f'(x) = \frac{2x + e^{x}}{2\sqrt{x^2 + e^{x}}} + 2\left(x^2 + e^{x}\right)\left(2x + e^{x}\right). \]

(b) \(x^2 + e^x\) appears twice in \(f'\) (and twice more in \(f\)), and \(2x + e^x\) appears twice. Evaluated literally, \(f\) needs 2 exponentials and \(f'\) needs 4, so 6 in total, for a quantity that only ever needs \(e^x\) once. For deeper compositions the written-out derivative grows much faster than the function: this is expression swell.

(c) With \(u' = 2x + e^x\),

\[ f'(x) = \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{u}} + 2u\right)u'. \]

At \(x = 0\): \(u = 1\), \(u' = 1\), so \(f(0) = 1 + 1 = \mathbf{2}\) and \(f'(0) = \left(\tfrac{1}{2} + 2\right)\cdot 1 = \mathbf{\tfrac{5}{2}}\).

At \(x = 1\): \(u = 1 + e \approx 3.71828\), \(u' = 2 + e \approx 4.71828\), so \(f(1) = \sqrt{u} + u^2 \approx \mathbf{15.75390}\) and

\[ f'(1) = \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1 + e}} + 2(1 + e)\right)(2 + e) \approx 7.69586 \times 4.71828 \approx \mathbf{36.31124}. \]

(d) \(\frac{f(1 + 10^{-5}) - f(1 - 10^{-5})}{2 \times 10^{-5}} \approx 36.31124\), in agreement.

Key insight: Naming each intermediate result once and reusing it is all it takes to keep the cost of a derivative close to the cost of the function; backpropagation and automatic differentiation are this idea made systematic.

P6.20 L3 · Application

Backpropagation through a two-layer model, by hand

Use the layered model of slide 239 with \(K = 2\):

\[ f_0 = x, \qquad f_1 = \operatorname{ReLU}(A_0 f_0 + b_0), \qquad f_2 = A_1 f_1 + b_1, \qquad L = (y - f_2)^2, \]

with

\[ x = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad A_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad A_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b_1 = 1, \quad y = 1. \]
