\[ H = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad f(\delta) \approx 0 + \delta_y + \tfrac{1}{2}(2\delta_x\delta_y) = \mathbf{\delta_y + \delta_x\delta_y}. \]

(b) With \(\delta = (0.1, 0.2)\): the model gives \(0.2 + 0.02 = \mathbf{0.22}\); the exact value is \(e^{0.1}\sin 0.2 = 0.219564\). The error is \(4.4 \times 10^{-4}\), of third order in \(\lVert \delta \rVert\).

(c) \(F(t) = e^t \sin 2t\), so

\[ F'(t) = e^t(\sin 2t + 2\cos 2t), \qquad F''(t) = e^t(4\cos 2t - 3\sin 2t), \]

giving \(F'(0) = 2\) and \(F''(0) = 4\). The formulas agree:

\[ hf_x + kf_y = 1 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 1 = 2, \qquad h^2 f_{xx} + 2hkf_{xy} + k^2 f_{yy} = 0 + 2 \cdot 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 + 0 = 4 . \]

(d) At \((0, \tfrac{\pi}{2})\): \(f = 1\), \(\nabla f = (1, 0)\), \(H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\), so

\[ f(p + \delta) \approx 1 + \delta_x + \tfrac{1}{2}(\delta_x^2 - \delta_y^2). \]

With \(\delta = (0.1, 0.1)\) the model gives \(1.1\); the exact value is \(e^{0.1}\cos 0.1 = 1.099650\).

Key insight: The gradient supplies the tilt and the Hessian the curvature of the local model; restricting to a line \(t \mapsto p + t(h, k)\) turns the two-variable expansion into the ordinary one-variable Taylor polynomial of \(F(t)\).

P7.13 L2 · Computation

Classify four critical points

Find and classify all critical points of

\[ f(x, y) = x^3 + y^3 - 3x - 12y , \]

and give the value of \(f\) at each.

Hint

The equations \(f_x = 0\) and \(f_y = 0\) decouple. Here \(f_{xy} = 0\), so \(D = f_{xx}f_{yy}\).

Answer & Key Insight

\(f_x = 3x^2 - 3 = 0\) gives \(x = \pm 1\); \(f_y = 3y^2 - 12 = 0\) gives \(y = \pm 2\). With \(f_{xx} = 6x\), \(f_{yy} = 6y\), \(f_{xy} = 0\), we have \(D = 36xy\).

Point \(f_{xx}\) \(f_{yy}\) \(D\) Type \(f\)
\((1, 2)\) 6 12 72 local minimum \(-18\)
\((-1, -2)\) \(-6\) \(-12\) 72 local maximum 18
\((1, -2)\) 6 \(-12\) \(-72\) saddle 14
\((-1, 2)\) \(-6\) 12 \(-72\) saddle \(-14\)

For example \(f(1, 2) = 1 + 8 - 3 - 24 = -18\).

Note that the saddle at \((1, -2)\) has a larger value (14) than the local minimum, and none of these extrema is global: \(f \to \pm\infty\) along the \(x\)-axis.

Key insight: With a diagonal Hessian the test reduces to reading signs: two positive curvatures give a minimum, two negative a maximum, mixed signs a saddle. "Local" means local; the cubic terms make every one of these points beatable far away.

P7.14 L3 · Application

Completing the square in \(Q\)

Let \(Q(h, k) = h^2 f_{xx} + 2hkf_{xy} + k^2 f_{yy}\), with the second partials evaluated at a critical point.

(a) Show that \(f_{xx}\,Q = (hf_{xx} + kf_{xy})^2 + (f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2)k^2\), and explain why this decides the sign of \(Q\) when \(f_{xx} \ne 0\) and \(D \ne 0\).

(b) Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 6xy + 4y^2 + 2x + 4y\). Find its critical point \(p\) and \(f(p)\), write \(Q\), and use the identity from (a) to classify \(p\). Give one direction \((h, k)\) in which \(f\) increases from \(p\) and one in which it decreases, with the exact changes \(f(p + (h, k)) - f(p)\). Along which lines through \(p\) is \(Q = 0\)?

(c) At another critical point the second partials are \(f_{xx} = 2\), \(f_{xy} = 1\), \(f_{yy} = 3\). Use the identity to show that \(Q > 0\) for every \((h, k) \ne (0, 0)\).

(d) The identity is useless when \(f_{xx} = 0\). Classify the critical point of \(f(x, y) = xy\) at the origin without it.

Hint

For (a), expand the right-hand side. For (b), \(f\) is quadratic, so its second-order Taylor expansion is exact: \(f(p + (h, k)) - f(p) = \tfrac{1}{2}Q\) with no intermediate point needed.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Expanding,

\[ \begin{aligned} (hf_{xx} + kf_{xy})^2 + (f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2)k^2 &= h^2 f_{xx}^2 + 2hkf_{xx}f_{xy} + k^2 f_{xy}^2 + k^2 f_{xx}f_{yy} - k^2 f_{xy}^2 \\ &= f_{xx}\big(h^2 f_{xx} + 2hkf_{xy} + k^2 f_{yy}\big) = f_{xx}\,Q . \end{aligned} \]

If \(D > 0\), the right-hand side is a sum of a square and a positive multiple of \(k^2\), so it is positive for \((h, k) \ne 0\) (if \(k = 0\) then \(h \ne 0\) and the square is \(h^2 f_{xx}^2 > 0\)). Hence \(Q\) has the sign of \(f_{xx}\): a minimum if \(f_{xx} > 0\), a maximum if \(f_{xx} < 0\). If \(D < 0\), taking \(k = 0\) makes the right-hand side positive, and taking \(h = -kf_{xy}/f_{xx}\), \(k \ne 0\), makes it negative, so \(Q\) takes both signs: a saddle.

(b) \(f_x = 2x + 6y + 2 = 0\) and \(f_y = 6x + 8y + 4 = 0\) give \(p = \left(-\tfrac{2}{5}, -\tfrac{1}{5}\right)\), with \(f(p) = -\tfrac{4}{5}\). The second partials are constant, \(f_{xx} = 2\), \(f_{xy} = 6\), \(f_{yy} = 8\), so

\[ Q = 2h^2 + 12hk + 8k^2, \qquad 2Q = (2h + 6k)^2 - 20k^2 . \]

\(D = 16 - 36 = -20 < 0\): a saddle. Because \(f\) is quadratic, \(f(p + (h, k)) - f(p) = \tfrac{1}{2}Q\) exactly:

  • \((h, k) = (1, 0)\): \(Q = 2\), so \(f\) increases by 1.
  • \((h, k) = (-3, 1)\) (this kills the square): \(Q = 18 - 36 + 8 = -10\), so \(f\) decreases by 5.

\(Q = 0\) when \(h^2 + 6hk + 4k^2 = 0\), that is along the lines \(h = (-3 \pm \sqrt{5})k\) through \(p\); they separate the "up" and "down" sectors of the saddle.

(c) \(2Q = (2h + k)^2 + (6 - 1)k^2 = (2h + k)^2 + 5k^2\). This is zero only if \(k = 0\) and then \(2h = 0\), so \(Q > 0\) for every \((h, k) \ne 0\), and the point is a strict local minimum.

(d) \(f = xy\) has \(f_{xx} = f_{yy} = 0\), \(f_{xy} = 1\), so \(Q = 2hk\) and \(D = -1\). Directly, \(Q(1, 1) = 2 > 0\) and \(Q(1, -1) = -2 < 0\): a saddle. (Completing the square with \(f_{yy}\) in place of \(f_{xx}\) fails too; the classification via \(D < 0\) does not need either.)

Key insight: Completing the square writes \(Q\) as "square plus \(D\) times \(k^2\)", so the sign of \(D\) decides whether \(Q\) can change sign. This is the two-variable version of the statement that the Hessian's definiteness decides the shape.

P7.15 L3 · Application

A full classification, and three inconclusive cases

(a) Find all real critical points of \(f(x, y) = x^4 + y^4 - 4xy\) and classify each with the second-derivative test. Give \(f\) at each.

(b) Show that each of

\[ g_1(x, y) = x^4 + y^2, \qquad g_2(x, y) = x^3 + y^2, \qquad g_3(x, y) = -x^4 - y^2 \]

has a critical point at the origin with \(D = 0\).

(c) Decide the nature of the origin for each \(g_i\) by a direct argument.

(d) \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) have the same Hessian at the origin. What does that tell you about the limits of a second-order test?

Hint

In (a), the first equation gives \(y = x^3\); substitute into the second. In (c), compare \(g_i(x, y)\) with \(g_i(0, 0) = 0\), and try moving along the \(x\)-axis.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(f_x = 4x^3 - 4y = 0\) and \(f_y = 4y^3 - 4x = 0\) give \(y = x^3\) and \(x^9 = x\), so \(x \in \{0, 1, -1\}\) and the real critical points are \((0, 0)\), \((1, 1)\), \((-1, -1)\). The Hessian is \(\begin{bmatrix} 12x^2 & -4 \\ -4 & 12y^2 \end{bmatrix}\).

  • \((0, 0)\): \(D = 0 \cdot 0 - 16 = -16 < 0\), saddle, \(f = 0\).
  • \((1, 1)\) and \((-1, -1)\): \(D = 144 - 16 = 128 > 0\) and \(f_{xx} = 12 > 0\), local minima, \(f = 1 + 1 - 4 = -2\).

(b) All three have \(\nabla g_i(0, 0) = 0\). Their Hessians at the origin are

\[ H_{g_1} = H_{g_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad H_{g_3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \]

so \(D = 0 \cdot (\pm 2) - 0 = 0\) in every case: the test is inconclusive.

(c)

  • \(g_1 = x^4 + y^2 \ge 0 = g_1(0, 0)\), with equality only at the origin: strict local (and global) minimum.
  • \(g_2(t, 0) = t^3\) is positive for \(t > 0\) and negative for \(t < 0\): not an extremum (it behaves like a degenerate saddle).
  • \(g_3 = -x^4 - y^2 \le 0\): strict local maximum.

(d) Any test that looks only at second derivatives sees \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) as identical, yet one has a minimum and the other does not. When \(D = 0\) the Hessian has a zero eigenvalue, and along that eigenvector (here the \(x\)-axis) the behaviour is decided by third- or higher-order Taylor terms, which the test ignores.

Key insight: \(D = 0\) does not mean "no extremum"; it means the quadratic model is flat in some direction, so you must look at higher-order terms or argue directly. Every outcome (minimum, maximum, neither) is possible.

9.C The Hessian (7.3)

P7.16 L1 · Foundation

The Hessian and definiteness: true or false

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each. "Critical point" means \(\nabla f = 0\), and \(f\) has continuous second partial derivatives.

(a) "The Hessian of \(f\) is a symmetric matrix."

(b) "A symmetric matrix with positive diagonal entries is positive definite."

(c) "A symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if all its leading principal minors are positive."

(d) "A symmetric matrix is negative definite if and only if all its leading principal minors are negative."

(e) "If \(f\) has a local minimum at a critical point, its Hessian there is positive definite."

(f) "If the Hessian at a critical point is positive definite, \(f\) has a strict local minimum there."

(g) "If the Hessian at a critical point has one positive and one negative eigenvalue, the point is a saddle."

(h) "If \(\det H > 0\) at a critical point of a function of two variables, the point is a local minimum."

Hint

Try \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), \(-I\), and the function \(x^4 + y^4\). Remember that the determinant is the product of the eigenvalues.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. Continuous second partials give \(f_{xy} = f_{yx}\) (slide 276; see P7.20 for what happens without continuity).

(b) False. \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) has eigenvalues 3 and \(-1\); \(x^\top A x = -2\) at \(x = (1, -1)\).

(c) True. That is Sylvester's criterion (slide 275).

(d) False. For negative definite the minors alternate in sign, starting negative (slide 276). \(-I_2\) has minors \(-1\) and \(+1\).

(e) False. \(x^4 + y^4\) has a strict minimum at the origin, but its Hessian there is the zero matrix. At a minimum the Hessian must be positive semidefinite; positive definite is sufficient, not necessary.

(f) True. Then \(Q = \delta^\top H \delta > 0\) for every \(\delta \ne 0\), and by continuity this persists at the nearby intermediate point in Taylor's theorem.

(g) True. Moving along the positive eigenvector increases \(f\) and moving along the negative one decreases it.

(h) False. \(\det H = \lambda_1\lambda_2 > 0\) only says the eigenvalues have the same sign. \(H = -I\) (from \(-x^2 - y^2\)) has \(\det H = 1\) and a maximum. You also need \(f_{xx} > 0\).

Key insight: The Hessian classifies a critical point through the signs of its eigenvalues; leading minors are a shortcut for reading those signs without computing the eigenvalues, and the determinant alone loses the overall sign.

P7.17 L1 · Foundation

Definiteness at a glance

Each matrix is the Hessian of some function at a critical point. Using leading minors or eigenvalues, say whether it is positive definite, negative definite, indefinite or only semidefinite, and what that means for the critical point.

\[ H_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}, \quad H_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad H_3 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad H_4 = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad H_5 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Hint

For a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, compute \(h_{11}\) and \(\det H\). For a diagonal matrix, the diagonal entries are the eigenvalues.

Answer & Key Insight
Hessian Leading minors Eigenvalues Definiteness Critical point
\(H_1\) 3, 15 3, 5 positive definite strict local minimum
\(H_2\) \(-2\), 5 \(\frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx -1.38, -3.62\) negative definite strict local maximum
\(H_3\) 1, \(-8\) 4, \(-2\) indefinite saddle
\(H_4\) 4, 0 5, 0 positive semidefinite inconclusive
\(H_5\) 2, \(-2\), \(-6\) 2, \(-1\), 3 indefinite saddle

For \(H_2\), the minors \(-2 < 0\) and \(5 > 0\) alternate starting negative, as negative definiteness requires. For \(H_4\), \(\det H_4 = 4 - 4 = 0\), so one eigenvalue is 0 and the second-order test cannot decide; the eigenvector for 0 is \((1, -2)\), the direction in which higher-order terms take over.

Key insight: A zero leading minor or a zero eigenvalue is the matrix form of "\(D = 0\)": the quadratic model is flat along some direction, so the Hessian alone cannot classify the point.

P7.18 L2 · Computation

Compute, check symmetry, classify

Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 y + xy^2 - 3xy\).

(a) Compute \(f_{xy} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) and \(f_{yx} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) and confirm they are equal. Write the Hessian \(H(x, y)\).

(b) Find all four critical points.

(c) Classify each one using the eigenvalues of \(H\), and confirm one of them with Sylvester's criterion. Give \(f\) at each.

Hint

Factor: \(f_x = y(2x + y - 3)\) and \(f_y = x(x + 2y - 3)\). Each factor can be zero independently.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(f_x = 2xy + y^2 - 3y\) and \(f_y = x^2 + 2xy - 3x\), so

\[ f_{xy} = 2x + 2y - 3 = f_{yx}, \qquad H(x, y) = \begin{bmatrix} 2y & 2x + 2y - 3 \\ 2x + 2y - 3 & 2x \end{bmatrix}. \]

(b) \(y(2x + y - 3) = 0\) and \(x(x + 2y - 3) = 0\). The four combinations give \((0, 0)\), \((0, 3)\), \((3, 0)\), \((1, 1)\) (the last from \(2x + y = 3\), \(x + 2y = 3\)).

(c)

Point \(H\) Eigenvalues Type \(f\)
\((0, 0)\) \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -3 \\ -3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) \(3, -3\) saddle 0
\((0, 3)\) \(\begin{bmatrix} 6 & 3 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) \(3 \pm 3\sqrt{2} \approx 7.24, -1.24\) saddle 0
\((3, 0)\) \(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 3 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\) \(3 \pm 3\sqrt{2}\) saddle 0
\((1, 1)\) \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) \(3, 1\) local minimum \(-1\)

Sylvester at \((1, 1)\): the leading minors are \(2 > 0\) and \(4 - 1 = 3 > 0\), so \(H\) is positive definite, confirming the minimum. At the three saddles \(\det H = -9 < 0\).

Since \(f = xy(x + y - 3)\), it vanishes on the three lines \(x = 0\), \(y = 0\), \(x + y = 3\); the saddles sit where those lines cross, and the minimum lies inside the triangle they enclose.

Key insight: Symmetry of the Hessian is what guarantees real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis (the spectral theorem of Module 4), so "classify by eigenvalue signs" always makes sense for a \(C^2\) function.

P7.19 L3 · Application

Three variables: Sylvester's criterion and eigenvalues

(a) Let \(f(x, y, z) = x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2 + 2xy + 2yz - 2x - 4z\). Find its critical point and the value of \(f\) there. Write the Hessian and classify the point using Sylvester's criterion. Then find the eigenvalues of the Hessian and confirm.

(b) Let \(g_a(x, y, z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + a(xy + yz + zx)\), which has a critical point at the origin for every real \(a\). Using the leading minors, find all \(a\) for which the origin is a strict local minimum. Find the eigenvalues of the Hessian and explain what happens at the boundary values of \(a\) and beyond them.

Hint

In (a) the gradient equations are linear. In (b), the Hessian is \(2I + a(J - I)\), where \(J\) is the all-ones matrix; \(J\) has eigenvalue 3 on \((1, 1, 1)\) and 0 on the plane orthogonal to it.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The gradient equations are

\[ 2x + 2y - 2 = 0, \qquad 2x + 4y + 2z = 0, \qquad 2y + 6z - 4 = 0, \]

with solution \((x, y, z) = \left(\tfrac{7}{2}, -\tfrac{5}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}\right)\) and \(f = -\tfrac{13}{2}\). The Hessian is constant:

\[ H = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \Delta_1 = 2, \quad \Delta_2 = 8 - 4 = 4, \quad \Delta_3 = \det H = 16 . \]

All three leading minors are positive, so \(H\) is positive definite and the point is a strict minimum (global, because \(f\) is quadratic). The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^3 - 12\lambda^2 + 36\lambda - 16 = (\lambda - 4)(\lambda^2 - 8\lambda + 4)\), so

\[ \lambda = 4, \quad 4 \pm 2\sqrt{3} \approx 7.464,\ 0.536 , \]

all positive. Check: their product is \(4 \cdot (16 - 12) = 16 = \det H\) and their sum is \(12 = \operatorname{tr} H\).

(b) The Hessian of \(g_a\) is \(\begin{bmatrix} 2 & a & a \\ a & 2 & a \\ a & a & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), with leading minors

\[ \Delta_1 = 2, \qquad \Delta_2 = 4 - a^2, \qquad \Delta_3 = 2(a - 2)^2(a + 1). \]

\(\Delta_2 > 0\) needs \(-2 < a < 2\), and \(\Delta_3 > 0\) then needs \(a > -1\). So the origin is a strict local minimum exactly for \(-1 < a < 2\).

The eigenvalues are \(2 + 2a\) (eigenvector \((1, 1, 1)\)) and \(2 - a\) (twice, on the plane \(x + y + z = 0\)), which are all positive exactly when \(-1 < a < 2\), in agreement.

  • \(a = 2\): eigenvalues \(6, 0, 0\); \(g_2 = (x + y + z)^2 \ge 0\), a minimum that is not strict (\(g_2 = 0\) on the whole plane \(x + y + z = 0\)).
  • \(a = -1\): eigenvalues \(0, 3, 3\); \(g_{-1} = \tfrac{1}{2}\big[(x - y)^2 + (y - z)^2 + (z - x)^2\big] \ge 0\), zero along the line \(x = y = z\): again a non-strict minimum.
  • \(a > 2\) or \(a < -1\): one eigenvalue is negative and the others positive, so the origin is a saddle.

Key insight: Sylvester's criterion and the eigenvalue test always agree for a symmetric matrix; the minors are quicker to compute, but the eigenvectors tell you the directions in which the function curves up, curves down or goes flat.

P7.20 L4 · Analysis

Why the Hessian is symmetric, and when it is not

The slides state (slide 276) that if \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable then \(\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x}\). Write \(f_{xy} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\big)\) and \(f_{yx} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\big(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\big)\).

(a) Verify \(f_{xy} = f_{yx}\) for \(f(x, y) = x^3 y^2 + e^{xy}\), and write the Hessian at \((1, 0)\).

(b) Now let

\[ g(x, y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{xy(x^2 - y^2)}{x^2 + y^2}, & (x, y) \ne (0, 0), \\ 0, & (x, y) = (0, 0). \end{cases} \]

Show that \(g_x(0, y) = -y\) and \(g_y(x, 0) = x\) for all \(x, y\), and deduce \(g_{xy}(0, 0)\) and \(g_{yx}(0, 0)\).

(c) For \((x, y) \ne (0, 0)\) one finds \(g_{xy} = g_{yx} = \frac{(x^2 - y^2)(x^4 + 10x^2y^2 + y^4)}{(x^2 + y^2)^3}\). Which hypothesis of the symmetry theorem fails at the origin?

(d) Explain why symmetry matters for the second-derivative test: what does \(\delta^\top H \delta\) see if \(H\) is not symmetric, and what property of eigenvalues would be lost?

Hint

For (b), \(g_x(0, y) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{g(h, y) - g(0, y)}{h}\) and \(g(0, y) = 0\). For (c), approach the origin along the two axes.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(f_x = 3x^2y^2 + ye^{xy}\) and \(f_y = 2x^3y + xe^{xy}\). Then

\[ f_{xy} = 6x^2 y + e^{xy} + xye^{xy}, \qquad f_{yx} = 6x^2 y + e^{xy} + xye^{xy}, \]

equal, as they must be for this smooth function. With \(f_{xx} = 6xy^2 + y^2 e^{xy}\) and \(f_{yy} = 2x^3 + x^2 e^{xy}\),

\[ H(1, 0) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(b) For \(y \ne 0\),

\[ g_x(0, y) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{1}{h}\cdot\frac{hy(h^2 - y^2)}{h^2 + y^2} = \frac{y(-y^2)}{y^2} = -y, \]

and \(g_x(0, 0) = \lim_{h \to 0}\frac{g(h, 0)}{h} = 0\), so \(g_x(0, y) = -y\) for every \(y\). By the same computation with the roles swapped, \(g_y(x, 0) = x\). Therefore

\[ g_{xy}(0, 0) = \frac{d}{dy}(-y)\Big|_{0} = \mathbf{-1}, \qquad g_{yx}(0, 0) = \frac{d}{dx}(x)\Big|_{0} = \mathbf{+1}. \]

The mixed partials at the origin differ.

(c) Along the \(x\)-axis (\(y = 0\)) the formula gives \(\frac{x^2 \cdot x^4}{x^6} = 1\); along the \(y\)-axis it gives \(\frac{-y^2 \cdot y^4}{y^6} = -1\). So the mixed partial has no limit at the origin: it is not continuous there, and \(g\) is not \(C^2\). That is exactly the hypothesis of the theorem (Clairaut's, or Schwarz's, theorem) that fails.

(d) A quadratic form only sees the symmetric part of its matrix: \(\delta^\top H \delta = \delta^\top \tfrac{1}{2}(H + H^\top)\delta\), because the antisymmetric part contributes \(\delta^\top A \delta = 0\). So a non-symmetric "Hessian" would carry information the second-order Taylor term never uses. More importantly, the eigenvalue test relies on the spectral theorem: a real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, so \(\delta^\top H \delta = \sum_i \lambda_i (q_i^\top\delta)^2\) and the signs of the \(\lambda_i\) decide everything. A non-symmetric matrix can have complex eigenvalues (\(\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) has \(\pm i\)), and then "the sign of an eigenvalue" means nothing.

Key insight: For the functions met in practice (polynomials, exponentials, smooth losses) the Hessian is symmetric, and that symmetry is what links curvature to real eigenvalues and orthogonal principal directions; the pathological \(g\) shows the continuity hypothesis is genuinely needed.

9.D Module 7 Capstone

P7.21 L4 · Analysis

Newton's method is "minimise the quadratic Taylor model"

(a) For a function of one variable, write the second-order Taylor model \(m(\delta) = f(x) + f'(x)\delta + \tfrac{1}{2}f''(x)\delta^2\) around the current point \(x\). Minimise \(m\) over \(\delta\) and derive the Newton update. When does \(m\) actually have a minimum?

(b) Do the same in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(m(\delta) = f(x) + \nabla f(x)^\top\delta + \tfrac{1}{2}\delta^\top H\delta\), and show that a single Newton step from any starting point lands exactly on the minimiser when \(f\) is a quadratic with positive definite Hessian. Illustrate with \(f(x, y) = 2x^2 + 2xy + y^2 - 2x\) from \((0, 0)\).

(c) Apply Newton's method to \(f(x) = e^x - 2x\) from \(x_0 = 0\) for three steps, and compare the errors \(\lvert x_t - \ln 2 \rvert\). What pattern do you see?

(d) What breaks: apply one Newton step to \(f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2\) from \(x_0 = 0.1\), and again from \(x_0 = 0.9\). Explain the difference using the sign of \(f''\).

Hint

Set \(m'(\delta) = 0\) (or \(\nabla m(\delta) = 0\)). For (b), a quadratic equals its own second-order Taylor model. For (d), \(f''(x) = 12x^2 - 4\) is negative for \(\lvert x \rvert < \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(m'(\delta) = f'(x) + f''(x)\delta = 0\) gives \(\delta = -\frac{f'(x)}{f''(x)}\), so

\[ x_{t+1} = x_t - \frac{f'(x_t)}{f''(x_t)} . \]

This stationary point of \(m\) is a minimum only if \(f''(x_t) > 0\). If \(f''(x_t) < 0\) the model is a downward parabola and the step goes to its maximum; if \(f''(x_t) = 0\) the step is undefined.

(b) \(\nabla m(\delta) = \nabla f(x) + H\delta = 0\) gives \(\delta = -H^{-1}\nabla f(x)\):

\[ x_{t+1} = x_t - H(x_t)^{-1}\nabla f(x_t), \]

a minimiser of \(m\) when \(H\) is positive definite. If \(f(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}x^\top A x + b^\top x + c\) with \(A\) positive definite, then \(\nabla f(x) = Ax + b\), \(H = A\), and \(x - A^{-1}(Ax + b) = -A^{-1}b\), the unique minimiser, whatever \(x\) was. For \(f = 2x^2 + 2xy + y^2 - 2x\):

\[ H = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \nabla f(0, 0) = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \delta = -H^{-1}\nabla f = \frac{1}{4}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

So \(x_1 = \mathbf{(1, -1)}\), and indeed \(\nabla f(1, -1) = (4 - 2 - 2,\ 2 - 2) = (0, 0)\).

(c) \(f'(x) = e^x - 2\), \(f''(x) = e^x > 0\), so \(x_{t+1} = x_t - 1 + 2e^{-x_t}\):

\(t\) \(x_t\) \(\lvert x_t - \ln 2 \rvert\)
0 0 0.693
1 1 0.307
2 \(\frac{2}{e} \approx 0.735759\) 0.0426
3 0.694042 \(8.95 \times 10^{-4}\)
4 0.6931476 \(4.0 \times 10^{-7}\)

Once close, the error is roughly squared at each step (\(0.0426 \to 9 \times 10^{-4} \to 4 \times 10^{-7}\)): quadratic convergence, because the model's error is third order in \(\delta\).

(d) \(f'(x) = 4x^3 - 4x\), \(f''(x) = 12x^2 - 4\). From \(x_0 = 0.1\): \(f''(0.1) = -3.88 < 0\), and

\[ x_1 = 0.1 - \frac{0.004 - 0.4}{0.12 - 4} = \mathbf{-0.00206}, \]

which jumps toward \(x = 0\), the local maximum of \(f\). From \(x_0 = 0.9\): \(f''(0.9) = 5.72 > 0\), and \(x_1 = 1.0196\), heading to the minimum at \(x = 1\). Newton's method looks for zeros of \(f'\), and it cannot tell a maximum from a minimum unless the Hessian is positive definite.

Key insight: Newton's method is "jump to the bottom of the local quadratic model". That is excellent when the model is a bowl (positive definite Hessian) and the current point is close, and it is actively harmful where the curvature is negative, which is why practical second-order methods add damping, line searches or a positive-definite correction.

P7.22 L5 · Mastery

The quadratic model of a trained network's loss, and the step-size bound

A model has been trained to parameters \(w^*\) with loss \(L(w^*) = 0.30\) and \(\nabla L(w^*) = 0\). In the two parameter directions you care about, the Hessian at \(w^*\) is

\[ H = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(a) Write the second-order Taylor model of \(L(w^* + \delta)\). Is \(w^*\) a local minimum? Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(H\).

(b) A compression scheme perturbs the weights by \(\delta = (0.1, -0.1)\); another by \(\delta = (0.1, 0.1)\). Both have the same length. Predict the loss after each and explain the difference.

(c) Near \(w^*\), gradient descent \(w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta\nabla L(w_t)\) acts on the model. Show that the error \(e_t = w_t - w^*\) obeys \(e_{t+1} = (I - \eta H)e_t\), and derive the condition on \(\eta\) for convergence. What happens at \(\eta = 0.3\)?

(d) Which fixed \(\eta\) gives the fastest worst-case convergence, and what is the contraction factor per step? Why is it the largest eigenvalue that limits \(\eta\) while the smallest limits the speed?

Hint

On the quadratic model, \(\nabla L(w^* + e) = He\). Expand \(e_t\) in the eigenvectors of \(H\): each component is multiplied by \(1 - \eta\lambda_i\) per step.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The linear term vanishes, so

\[ L(w^* + \delta) \approx 0.30 + \tfrac{1}{2}\delta^\top H \delta . \]

\(H\) has leading minors \(5 > 0\) and \(25 - 9 = 16 > 0\), so it is positive definite and \(w^*\) is a strict local minimum. Its eigenpairs are \(\lambda_1 = 8\) on \((1, 1)\) and \(\lambda_2 = 2\) on \((1, -1)\).

(b) With \(\delta = (0.1, -0.1)\) (the flat direction): \(\delta^\top H\delta = 0.05 - 0.06 + 0.05 = 0.04\), so \(L \approx 0.30 + 0.02 = \mathbf{0.32}\). With \(\delta = (0.1, 0.1)\) (the sharp direction): \(\delta^\top H\delta = 0.05 + 0.06 + 0.05 = 0.16\), so \(L \approx 0.30 + 0.08 = \mathbf{0.38}\). The same-sized perturbation costs four times as much along the eigenvector with four times the curvature (\(\tfrac{1}{2}\lambda\lVert\delta\rVert^2\) with \(\lVert\delta\rVert^2 = 0.02\)). This is why pruning and quantisation methods (for example "optimal brain damage"-style saliencies) weight each change by curvature.

(c) On the model, \(\nabla L(w^* + e) = He\), so \(e_{t+1} = e_t - \eta He_t = (I - \eta H)e_t\). Writing \(e_t\) in the eigenbasis, the component along \(q_i\) is multiplied by \(1 - \eta\lambda_i\) each step. Convergence for every starting error needs \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_i \rvert < 1\) for all \(i\), that is

\[ 0 < \eta < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}} = \frac{2}{8} = \mathbf{0.25}. \]

At \(\eta = 0.3\) the factors are \(1 - 2.4 = -1.4\) and \(1 - 0.6 = 0.4\): the component along \((1, 1)\) flips sign and grows by 40% each step, so gradient descent diverges (oscillating across the valley), even though it would be fine along \((1, -1)\).

(d) The worst-case factor \(\max_i \lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_i \rvert\) is minimised when \(1 - \eta\lambda_{\min} = -(1 - \eta\lambda_{\max})\), giving

\[ \eta^* = \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max} + \lambda_{\min}} = \frac{2}{10} = \mathbf{0.2}, \qquad \text{factor} = \frac{\lambda_{\max} - \lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max} + \lambda_{\min}} = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1} = \mathbf{0.6} \]

with condition number \(\kappa = 4\). The largest eigenvalue caps \(\eta\) because the steepest direction must not overshoot; once \(\eta\) is capped at about \(\frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}\), progress along the flattest direction is only about \(\eta\lambda_{\min} \approx \frac{2\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}}\) per step. Feature scaling, preconditioning and adaptive methods all aim to make the eigenvalues more equal.

Key insight: Near a trained point the loss is, to second order, the bowl \(\tfrac{1}{2}\delta^\top H\delta\). Its eigenvalues say which perturbations are cheap, how large a learning rate is safe (\(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\)) and how slow convergence will be (governed by \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\)). Module 8 builds directly on this picture.

P7.23 L5 · Mastery

First-order approximations that ML uses every day

Each part uses a one- or two-term Maclaurin polynomial. For each, quantify the error with the Lagrange remainder or an exact comparison, and say when the approximation stops being safe.

(a) Log-returns. A price moves from 100 to 102, a simple return of \(R = 0.02\). Analysts often use the log-return \(r = \ln(1 + R)\) and treat it as \(\approx R\). Bound \(R - \ln(1 + R)\) using the remainder of \(T_1\), and compare with the true value. Repeat for \(R = -0.02\) and for \(R = 0.5\). Then show why log-returns, not simple returns, add up over time, using a \(+10\%\) day followed by a \(-10\%\) day.

(b) Cosine similarity of nearly parallel embeddings. Use \(\cos\theta \approx 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2}\) to estimate the angle between two embeddings whose cosine similarity is 0.99, and bound the error of the approximation at \(\theta = 0.1\). What does the quadratic behaviour mean for using \(1 - \cos\theta\) as a distance?

(c) Softmax at high temperature. For logits \(z \in \mathbb{R}^K\), \(p_i(T) = \frac{e^{z_i/T}}{\sum_j e^{z_j/T}}\). Expand in \(\varepsilon = \frac{1}{T}\) to first order to show \(p_i \approx \frac{1}{K} + \frac{z_i - \bar{z}}{KT}\), where \(\bar{z}\) is the mean logit. Test it for \(z = (2, 1, 0)\) at \(T = 10\), and describe what happens at \(T = 1\) and \(T = 0.1\).

(d) The tail of the logistic loss. The logistic loss of a correctly classified point with margin \(m\) is \(\ln(1 + e^{-m})\). Using \(\ln(1 + u) \approx u\) with \(u = e^{-m}\), show that for large margins it behaves like the exponential loss \(e^{-m}\), and give the error at \(m = 3\).

Hint

For \(f(u) = \ln(1 + u)\), \(T_1(u) = u\) and \(R_1(u) = -\frac{u^2}{2(1 + c)^2}\) with \(c\) between 0 and \(u\). For (c), differentiate \(p_i\) with respect to \(\varepsilon\) and evaluate at \(\varepsilon = 0\), where every \(p_j = \frac{1}{K}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) From the remainder, \(R - \ln(1 + R) = \frac{R^2}{2(1 + c)^2}\) with \(c\) between 0 and \(R\), which is always positive: the log-return is smaller than the simple return.

  • \(R = 0.02\): the error lies between \(\frac{0.0004}{2(1.02)^2} = 1.92 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(\frac{0.0004}{2} = 2.00 \times 10^{-4}\). True: \(\ln 1.02 = 0.0198026\), error \(1.97 \times 10^{-4}\), about 1% of \(R\).
  • \(R = -0.02\): now \(1 + c \in (0.98, 1)\), so the error lies between \(2.00 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(2.08 \times 10^{-4}\). True: \(\ln 0.98 = -0.0202027\), error \(2.03 \times 10^{-4}\).
  • \(R = 0.5\): \(\ln 1.5 = 0.405\) against 0.5, an error of 0.095, almost 20%. The approximation is only safe for small returns; the error grows like \(R^2/2\).

Over two days, \(+10\%\) then \(-10\%\) leaves \(100 \times 1.1 \times 0.9 = 99\). The simple returns sum to 0, which is wrong; the log-returns sum to \(\ln 1.1 + \ln 0.9 = \ln 0.99 = -0.01005\), exactly the log of the total change, because \(\ln\) turns products into sums.

(b) \(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} = 0.99\) gives \(\theta \approx \sqrt{0.02} = \mathbf{0.1414}\) rad (about \(8.1^\circ\)); the exact \(\arccos 0.99 = 0.14154\). Since \(1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2} = T_2 = T_3\) for \(\cos\), the error is at most \(\frac{\theta^4}{24} = 4.17 \times 10^{-6}\) at \(\theta = 0.1\) (where \(1 - \cos 0.1 = 0.0049958\) against \(0.005\)). Because \(1 - \cos\theta \approx \frac{\theta^2}{2}\), cosine distance is quadratic in the angle: an \(8^\circ\) disagreement looks like a 1% change, and differences between "very similar" items are compressed near similarity 1. If you need a distance that is linear in the angle, use \(\theta = \arccos(\cdot)\) itself.

(c) Write \(p_i = \frac{e^{\varepsilon z_i}}{S}\) with \(S = \sum_j e^{\varepsilon z_j}\). Then

\[ \frac{dp_i}{d\varepsilon} = \frac{z_i e^{\varepsilon z_i}S - e^{\varepsilon z_i}\sum_j z_j e^{\varepsilon z_j}}{S^2} = p_i\Big(z_i - \sum_j p_j z_j\Big), \]

which at \(\varepsilon = 0\) (where \(p_j = \frac{1}{K}\)) equals \(\frac{1}{K}(z_i - \bar{z})\). Hence

\[ p_i \approx \frac{1}{K} + \frac{z_i - \bar{z}}{KT}. \]

For \(z = (2, 1, 0)\), \(\bar{z} = 1\), \(K = 3\), \(T = 10\): the approximation gives \((0.3667, 0.3333, 0.3000)\), against the exact \((0.3672, 0.3322, 0.3006)\). At \(T = 1\) the exact softmax is \((0.665, 0.245, 0.090)\), far from linear, and at \(T = 0.1\) it is \((0.99995, 4.5 \times 10^{-5}, 2 \times 10^{-9})\), essentially the argmax. So high temperature makes the output uniform plus a small correction proportional to the centred logits, which is why distillation with large \(T\) transfers the logit differences of the teacher.

(d) With \(u = e^{-m}\), \(\ln(1 + u) = u - \frac{u^2}{2(1 + c)^2}\) for some \(c \in (0, u)\), so \(\ln(1 + e^{-m}) \approx e^{-m}\) with an error below \(\frac{e^{-2m}}{2}\). At \(m = 3\): \(\ln(1 + e^{-3}) = 0.048587\), \(e^{-3} = 0.049787\); the error is \(1.20 \times 10^{-3}\) (bound \(\frac{e^{-6}}{2} = 1.24 \times 10^{-3}\)), a relative error of about 2.5%, shrinking like \(e^{-m}/2\). Well-classified points therefore contribute to logistic regression almost exactly as they would to an exponential-loss (boosting-style) objective.

Key insight: "\(\ln(1 + x) \approx x\)", "\(\cos\theta \approx 1 - \theta^2/2\)" and "softmax is nearly uniform at high \(T\)" are all first- or second-order Taylor polynomials. The remainder tells you both how big the error is (second order in the small quantity) and the regime where it is no longer small.

P7.24 L5 · Mastery

Misconception traps: a code review of five claims

A colleague's notes on an optimisation project contain the five claims below. For each, decide whether it is right, give a concrete counterexample or supporting computation, and write a corrected statement.

(1) "Training stopped because \(\lVert\nabla L\rVert\) was below \(10^{-8}\), so we are at a minimum." (At the final point the Hessian, restricted to two directions, is \(\operatorname{diag}(4, -0.5)\).)

(2) "If a Taylor polynomial is a decent approximation, adding more terms can only make it better." (Test with \(\ln(1 + x)\) at \(x = 1.5\) and with \(e^x\) at \(x = -10\).)

(3) "At a critical point where \(f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2 = 0\), there is no extremum."

(4) "All diagonal entries of the Hessian are positive, so the loss is locally convex here."

(5) "The Lagrange bound says 44 terms are needed for \(e^{10}\) to \(10^{-6}\), so 43 terms will certainly be worse than \(10^{-6}\)."

Hint

For claim 1, move a distance 0.2 along the eigenvector with eigenvalue \(-0.5\) and use the quadratic model. For claim 2, compute \(T_1, \dots, T_8\) of \(\ln(1 + x)\) at \(1.5\) and compare with \(\ln 2.5 = 0.9163\).

Answer & Key Insight

(1) Wrong. A tiny gradient only says the point is (nearly) stationary. With \(H = \operatorname{diag}(4, -0.5)\) it is a saddle: moving by \(\delta = (0, 0.2)\) changes the loss by about \(\tfrac{1}{2}(-0.5)(0.2)^2 = -0.01\), a decrease. Corrected: a stationary point is a local minimum if the Hessian is positive definite there; check the smallest eigenvalue (in large models, by Hessian-vector products and power iteration on \(-H\) or \(\lambda I - H\)). Saddles with a few negative directions are common in high-dimensional losses, and noise in SGD helps escape them.

(2) Wrong. For \(\ln(1 + x)\) at \(x = 1.5\), outside the interval of convergence \((-1, 1]\):

\(n\) 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8
\(T_n(1.5)\) 1.500 0.375 1.500 0.234 1.753 \(-0.145\) 2.296 \(-0.908\)
error 0.584 \(-0.541\) 0.584 \(-0.682\) 0.837 \(-1.062\) 1.379 \(-1.824\)

The errors oscillate and grow without bound. Even for \(e^x\), which converges everywhere, \(T_1(-10) = -9\) and \(T_2(-10) = 41\) are both terrible and the second is worse, because the terms \(\frac{10^k}{k!}\) grow until \(k = 9\) (P7.9). Corrected: inside the region where the remainder tends to 0, the error eventually goes to 0 as \(n\) grows; it need not decrease at every step, and outside that region extra terms can make things worse.

(3) Wrong. \(D = 0\) makes the test inconclusive: at the origin \(x^4 + y^4\) has a minimum, \(-x^4 - y^4\) a maximum and \(x^3 + y^2\) neither (P7.15). Corrected: when \(D = 0\), examine higher-order terms along the null direction of the Hessian, or argue directly.

(4) Wrong. \(H = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) (from \(x^2 + 3xy + y^2\)) has positive diagonal but eigenvalues 5 and \(-1\), and \(f\) decreases along \((1, -1)\). Corrected: local convexity needs \(H\) positive semidefinite (all eigenvalues \(\ge 0\)); by Sylvester's criterion, positive definiteness needs all leading minors positive, including \(\det H = 4 - 9 = -5\), which fails here.

(5) Wrong. The Lagrange bound is only an upper bound, because it replaces \(e^{c}\) by its worst case \(e^{10}\). For \(e^{10}\) the bound first drops below \(10^{-6}\) at degree 43 (44 terms), but the true error already does so at degree 36 (P7.9). Corrected: the bound guarantees accuracy when it is small enough; when it is not, the true error may still be small. The bound is tight only when \(f^{(n+1)}\) is nearly constant on the interval (as for \(\cos\) near 0 in P7.6).

Key insight: Each trap confuses a necessary condition, a sufficient condition or an upper bound with an "if and only if". A zero gradient is necessary, a positive definite Hessian is sufficient, \(D = 0\) decides nothing, and a remainder bound guarantees but does not measure.

PART 10 — Module 8: Gradient Descent

Conventions used throughout this module (they follow the Topic 9 deck, slides 279–310): \(f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}\) is differentiable, and, as in the deck, its gradient \(\nabla f\) is a row vector, so the gradient-descent update is

\[ x_{i+1} = x_i - \eta\, \big(\nabla f(x_i)\big)^\top . \]

The deck calls the step size \(\gamma\) on slides 287–290 and the learning rate \(\alpha\) on slides 292–307; this module writes \(\eta\) for a fixed step and \(\eta_t\) or \(\alpha_t\) for a schedule, and they all mean the same thing. When a column is more convenient (for example in \(g^\top H g\)), \(g = (\nabla f)^\top\) denotes the gradient written as a column. \(H = \nabla^2 f\) is the Hessian; for a quadratic \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^\top A x + b^\top x\) with \(A\) symmetric, \(\nabla f = x^\top A + b^\top\) and \(H = A\). The eigenvalues of a symmetric positive definite \(H\) are \(0 < \lambda_{\min} = \lambda_d \le \dots \le \lambda_1 = \lambda_{\max}\), and \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\) is its condition number. A search direction is \(g_t\), and a line search chooses the scalar \(\alpha_t\) in \(w_{t+1} = w_t + \alpha_t g_t\) (slide 296). Exact fractions are given first, decimals alongside, and numbers are rounded only at the end.

10.A Unconstrained Optimisation (8.1)

P8.1 L1 · Foundation

Unconstrained optimisation: true or false

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "In an unconstrained problem every \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is allowed, and at a local minimum of a differentiable \(f\) the gradient is zero."

(b) "If \(\nabla f(x^*) = 0\), then \(x^*\) is a local minimum of \(f\)."

(c) "If \(\nabla f(x) \ne 0\), a small enough step from \(x\) in the direction \(-(\nabla f(x))^\top\) lowers \(f\)."

(d) "For a function of one variable, if \(f'(x_0) = 0\) and \(f''(x_0)\) is not negative, then \(x_0\) is a local minimum."

(e) "Minimising \(f(x) = x^2\) subject to \(x \ge 1\) is an unconstrained problem because it has only one variable."

(f) "A local minimum of a differentiable function is always its global minimum."

Hint

For (b) and (d), test \(f(x) = x^3\) and \(f(x) = -x^4\) at \(x = 0\). For (c), compute the directional derivative of \(f\) along \(-(\nabla f)^\top\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. With no constraints every point is feasible, so a local minimum is an interior point and the first-order condition \(\nabla f(x^*) = 0\) must hold (slide 283).

(b) False. \(f(x) = -x^2\) has \(f'(0) = 0\) at a maximum, and \(f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2\) has \(\nabla f(0, 0) = 0\) at a saddle. A zero gradient only marks a stationary point.

(c) True. The rate of change of \(f\) along \(d = -(\nabla f)^\top\) is

\[ \nabla f(x)\, d = -\lVert \nabla f(x) \rVert^2 < 0, \]

so \(f\) decreases for all small enough step sizes. This is the whole idea behind gradient descent.

(d) False. When \(f''(x_0) = 0\) the test says nothing: \(x^3\) has an inflection point at 0, \(x^4\) a minimum and \(-x^4\) a maximum, and all three have \(f'(0) = f''(0) = 0\). Only \(f''(x_0) > 0\) guarantees a minimum. (Slide 285 says "otherwise it is a local minimum", which silently includes the inconclusive case \(f'' = 0\).)

(e) False. The restriction \(x \ge 1\) is a constraint. Its minimiser is \(x = 1\), where \(f'(1) = 2 \ne 0\): at a constrained optimum the gradient need not vanish.

(f) False. The quartic in P8.2 has two local minima with different values. A local minimum is guaranteed to be global only under extra structure such as convexity.

Key insight: \(\nabla f = 0\) is necessary for an unconstrained local minimum but not sufficient, and even a genuine local minimum need not be the global one.

P8.2 L2 · Computation

Stationary points of a quartic loss

Let \(l(x) = 3x^4 - 4x^3 - 12x^2 + 5\).

(a) Find \(l'(x)\) and all stationary points.

(b) Classify each stationary point with the second-derivative test.

(c) Compute \(l\) at each stationary point and identify the global minimum. Explain why a global minimum exists.

Hint

\(l'(x)\) has a common factor \(12x\); the remaining quadratic factorises over the integers.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Differentiating and factorising,

\[ l'(x) = 12x^3 - 12x^2 - 24x = 12x(x^2 - x - 2) = 12x(x - 2)(x + 1), \]

so the stationary points are \(x = -1,\ 0,\ 2\).

(b) The second derivative is \(l''(x) = 36x^2 - 24x - 24\):

\[ l''(-1) = 36, \qquad l''(0) = -24, \qquad l''(2) = 72 . \]

So \(x = -1\) and \(x = 2\) are local minima, and \(x = 0\) is a local maximum.

(c) The values are

\[ l(-1) = 0, \qquad l(0) = 5, \qquad l(2) = -27 . \]

The global minimum is \(l(2) = -27\). A global minimum exists because the leading term \(3x^4\) makes \(l(x) \to \infty\) as \(\lvert x \rvert \to \infty\), so the minimum over \(\mathbb{R}\) is attained at one of the stationary points, and \(-27\) is the smallest of their values. The local minimum at \(x = -1\) is a trap: a descent method started to its left (P8.30) settles there with loss 0 instead of \(-27\).

Key insight: A cubic gradient has up to three zeros, giving at most two minima separated by a maximum; the second derivative classifies them, but only comparing values identifies the global one.

P8.3 L2 · Computation

A line fit as an unconstrained minimisation

Fit \(\hat{y} = ax + b\) to the four points \((1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 6)\) by minimising

\[ L(a, b) = \sum_{i=1}^{4} \big(y_i - (a x_i + b)\big)^2 . \]

(a) Write \(\nabla L = \big(\frac{\partial L}{\partial a}, \frac{\partial L}{\partial b}\big)\) in terms of \(a\) and \(b\).

(b) Solve \(\nabla L = 0\) for \(a\) and \(b\), and compute the minimum loss.

(c) Find the Hessian of \(L\) and use it to confirm that the stationary point is a minimum.

(d) Evaluate \(\nabla L(0, 0)\). In which direction would a gradient-descent step from \((0, 0)\) move?

Hint

\(\frac{\partial L}{\partial a} = -2\sum x_i(y_i - a x_i - b)\) and \(\frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = -2\sum (y_i - a x_i - b)\). You need \(\sum x_i = 10\), \(\sum x_i^2 = 30\), \(\sum y_i = 16\) and \(\sum x_i y_i = 47\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Using the sums in the hint,

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} = 60a + 20b - 94, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b} = 20a + 8b - 32 . \]

(b) Setting both to zero gives \(30a + 10b = 47\) and \(10a + 4b = 16\). From the second, \(b = (16 - 10a)/4\); substituting, \(30a + 40 - 25a = 47\), so

\[ a = \tfrac{7}{5} = 1.4, \qquad b = \tfrac{1}{2} = 0.5 . \]

The fitted line is \(\hat{y} = 1.4x + 0.5\). Its residuals are \(0.1, -0.3, 0.3, -0.1\), so the minimum loss is \(L = 0.01 + 0.09 + 0.09 + 0.01 = \tfrac{1}{5} = 0.2\).

(c) The Hessian is constant:

\[ H = \begin{bmatrix} 60 & 20 \\ 20 & 8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad H_{11} = 60 > 0, \qquad \det H = 480 - 400 = 80 > 0, \]

so \(H\) is positive definite and \((1.4, 0.5)\) is the unique (global) minimum. Its eigenvalues are \(34 \pm 2\sqrt{269}\), about \(66.80\) and \(1.198\).

(d) \(\nabla L(0, 0) = (-94, -32)\). A gradient-descent step moves along \(-(\nabla L)^\top = (94, 32)\), so it increases both \(a\) and \(b\), towards the minimiser.

Key insight: Least squares is an unconstrained minimisation whose loss is a convex quadratic, so \(\nabla L = 0\) (the normal equations) gives the global minimum directly; gradient descent is needed only when such a closed form is unavailable or too expensive.

10.B The Gradient-descent Iteration (8.2)

P8.4 L1 · Foundation

The gradient-descent step: true or false

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "In the deck's notation \(\nabla f(x)\) is a row vector, so the update \(x_{i+1} = x_i - \gamma (\nabla f(x_i))^\top\) needs the transpose to subtract it from the column \(x_i\)."

(b) "If \(\nabla f(x_0) \ne 0\) and \(\gamma > 0\) is small enough, then \(f(x_1) < f(x_0)\)."

(c) "For any fixed \(\gamma > 0\), however large, one gradient step satisfies \(f(x_1) \le f(x_0)\)."

(d) "With a suitable step size, gradient descent always converges to the global minimum."

(e) "The heuristic 'if a step increases \(f\), undo it and halve the step size' guarantees that the iterates converge to a minimum."

(f) "If gradient descent lands exactly on a point with \(\nabla f = 0\), it stops moving, even if that point is a saddle."

Hint

For (c), try \(f(x) = x^2\) from \(x_0 = 1\) with \(\gamma = 2\). For (e), separate "the values \(f(x_i)\) decrease" from "the points \(x_i\) approach a minimiser".

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. \(x_i\) is a column in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\nabla f(x_i)\) is \(1 \times d\), so its transpose is what is subtracted (slide 287).

(b) True. To first order \(f(x_1) \approx f(x_0) - \gamma \lVert \nabla f(x_0) \rVert^2\), and the negative first-order term dominates the \(O(\gamma^2)\) remainder when \(\gamma\) is small.

(c) False. For \(f(x) = x^2\), \(x_0 = 1\), \(\gamma = 2\): \(x_1 = 1 - 2 \cdot 2 = -3\) and \(f\) rises from 1 to 9. The guarantee in (b) is only for small steps.

(d) False. Gradient descent follows the local slope, so it reaches a stationary point near where it starts, typically a local minimum (slide 287 says "some local minimum"). P8.30 shows it stopping at the non-global minimum of the quartic in P8.2.

(e) False. The heuristic guarantees only that \(f(x_i)\) never increases (slide 289's "monotonic convergence" means this). The iterates can still stall at a saddle, a plateau or a local minimum.

(f) True. The update is \(x - \gamma \cdot 0 = x\). Saddles are unstable, so a tiny perturbation (or SGD noise) usually escapes them, but exact gradient descent does not.

Key insight: A gradient step is guaranteed to help only locally and only for small enough steps; descent of \(f\) is not the same as convergence to the global minimum.

P8.5 L2 · Computation

One parabola, five step sizes

Let \(f(x) = (x - 3)^2\) and start gradient descent at \(x_0 = 0\).

(a) Show that one step with step size \(\eta\) gives \(x_{k+1} - 3 = (1 - 2\eta)(x_k - 3)\).

(b) Compute \(x_1, x_2, x_3\) and \(f(x_3)\) for \(\eta = 0.25\), \(0.75\), \(1\) and \(1.25\). Describe each behaviour.

(c) For which \(\eta > 0\) does the iteration converge? Which \(\eta\) is best?

(d) Apply the halve-on-increase heuristic to \(\eta = 1.25\): take the step, and if \(f\) increases undo it and halve \(\eta\). What is the accepted \(x_1\)?

Hint

The distance to the minimiser is multiplied by the same factor \(1 - 2\eta\) at every step; look at its sign and its size.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Since \(f'(x) = 2(x - 3)\),

\[ x_{k+1} = x_k - 2\eta(x_k - 3) \quad\Rightarrow\quad x_{k+1} - 3 = (1 - 2\eta)(x_k - 3). \]

(b) With \(x_0 - 3 = -3\):

\(\eta\) \(1 - 2\eta\) \(x_1\) \(x_2\) \(x_3\) \(f(x_3)\) behaviour
0.25 0.5 1.5 2.25 2.625 \(\tfrac{9}{64} \approx 0.141\) monotone convergence from one side
0.75 \(-0.5\) 4.5 2.25 3.375 \(\tfrac{9}{64} \approx 0.141\) overshoots, oscillates, converges
1 \(-1\) 6 0 6 9 bounces between 0 and 6 forever
1.25 \(-1.5\) 7.5 \(-3.75\) 13.125 \(\tfrac{6561}{64} \approx 102.5\) oscillates and diverges

Note that \(\eta = 0.25\) and \(\eta = 0.75\) give the same \(f\) values: only \(\lvert 1 - 2\eta \rvert\) matters for the error size.

(c) Convergence needs \(\lvert 1 - 2\eta \rvert < 1\), that is \(0 < \eta < 1\). Here \(f'' = 2\), so this is \(\eta < 2/f''\). The best step is \(\eta = 0.5\), which makes the factor 0 and lands on \(x = 3\) in one step (it equals \(1/f''\), the Newton step).

(d) With \(\eta = 1.25\), \(x_1 = 7.5\) and \(f\) rises from 9 to 20.25, so the step is undone and \(\eta = 0.625\). Then \(1 - 2\eta = -0.25\), and \(x_1 = 3 + (-0.25)(-3) = 3.75\) with \(f(x_1) = \tfrac{9}{16} = 0.5625 < 9\), which is accepted.

Key insight: On a quadratic, gradient descent multiplies the error by \(1 - \eta f''\) at each step: below \(1/f''\) it creeps in from one side, between \(1/f''\) and \(2/f''\) it oscillates inward, and beyond \(2/f''\) it blows up.

P8.6 L3 · Application

Converge, zig-zag, diverge on \(x^2 + 4y^2\)

Let \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 4y^2\) and start at \((x_0, y_0) = (4, 1)\), where \(f = 20\).

(a) Write the gradient-descent update for each coordinate separately, with a fixed step \(\eta\).

(b) Run three iterations for each of \(\eta = 0.1\), \(\eta = 0.2\) and \(\eta = 0.3\), recording the point and \(f\) after each step.

(c) Describe the three behaviours and explain them using the Hessian.

(d) After one step, \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(\eta = 0.3\) give the same value of \(f\). Why is one step not enough to judge a learning rate?

Hint

\(\nabla f = (2x, 8y)\), so each coordinate is multiplied by its own constant factor at every step.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The coordinates decouple:

\[ x_{k+1} = (1 - 2\eta)\, x_k, \qquad y_{k+1} = (1 - 8\eta)\, y_k . \]

(b) The factors are \((0.8, 0.2)\), \((0.6, -0.6)\) and \((0.4, -1.4)\):

\(\eta\) step 1 step 2 step 3 \(f\) after steps 1, 2, 3
0.1 \((3.2, 0.2)\) \((2.56, 0.04)\) \((2.048, 0.008)\) 10.4, 6.56, 4.195
0.2 \((2.4, -0.6)\) \((1.44, 0.36)\) \((0.864, -0.216)\) 7.2, 2.592, 0.933
0.3 \((1.6, -1.4)\) \((0.64, 1.96)\) \((0.256, -2.744)\) 10.4, 15.78, 30.18

(c) The Hessian is \(H = \operatorname{diag}(2, 8)\), so \(\lambda_{\max} = 8\) and the stability bound is \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max} = 0.25\).

  • \(\eta = 0.1\): converges without oscillation. The steep direction \(y\) is killed fast (factor 0.2), but the shallow direction \(x\) crawls (factor 0.8), so after three steps \(f\) is still 4.2.
  • \(\eta = 0.2\): converges with a zig-zag. \(y\) flips sign every step (factor \(-0.6\)) while \(x\) shrinks by 0.6. Both errors shrink at the same rate, so this is in fact the best fixed step, \(\eta = 2/(\lambda_{\min} + \lambda_{\max}) = 2/10\), and \(f\) falls by \(0.6^2 = 0.36\) per step.
  • \(\eta = 0.3\): diverges. \(\eta > 0.25\) gives \(\lvert 1 - 8\eta \rvert = 1.4 > 1\), so \(y\) oscillates with growing amplitude even though \(x\) still converges. One unstable direction is enough to ruin the run.

(d) At step 1, \(\eta = 0.1\) gives \(f = 3.2^2 + 4(0.2)^2 = 10.24 + 0.16\) and \(\eta = 0.3\) gives \(f = 1.6^2 + 4(-1.4)^2 = 2.56 + 7.84\); both equal 10.4. The first step of the divergent run looks fine because the stable \(x\)-direction dominates \(f\) at the start. Only after a few steps does the growing \(y\)-oscillation take over, so a learning rate should be judged on a trend of several iterations, not on one.

Key insight: The largest curvature sets the speed limit \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\), and the smallest curvature then decides how slowly the run finishes; with unequal curvatures even the best fixed step zig-zags.

P8.7 L3 · Application

Gradient descent on a coupled quadratic

Let \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^\top A x + b^\top x\) with

\[ A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad b = \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \]

(a) Write the row gradient \(\nabla f(x)\) and find the minimiser \(x^*\) and the minimum value \(f(x^*)\).

(b) Run three gradient-descent steps with \(\eta = 0.2\). Record \(\nabla f(x_k)\), \(x_{k+1}\) and \(f(x_{k+1})\) at each step.

(c) Find the largest constant step size for which gradient descent converges from every starting point.

Hint

\(\nabla f(x) = x^\top A + b^\top\). For (c), compute the eigenvalues of \(A\) from \(\lambda^2 - 5\lambda + 5 = 0\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The gradient is \(\nabla f(x) = x^\top A + b^\top = (3x_1 + x_2 - 5,\ x_1 + 2x_2 - 5)\). Setting it to zero gives \(Ax^* = -b\):

\[ x^* = -A^{-1}b = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad f(x^*) = \tfrac{1}{2}b^\top x^* = \tfrac{1}{2}(-5 - 10) = -\tfrac{15}{2}. \]

So \(x^* = (1, 2)\) and \(f(x^*) = -7.5\). (At a minimiser \(Ax^* = -b\), so \(f(x^*) = \frac{1}{2}x^{*\top}(-b) + b^\top x^* = \frac{1}{2}b^\top x^*\).) \(A\) is positive definite (\(3 > 0\), \(\det A = 5 > 0\)), so this is the global minimum.

(b) The update is \(x_{k+1} = x_k - 0.2\,(\nabla f(x_k))^\top\), and \(f(x_0) = 0\):

\(k\) \(x_k\) \(\nabla f(x_k)\) \(x_{k+1}\) \(f(x_{k+1})\)
0 \((0, 0)\) \((-5, -5)\) \((1, 1)\) \(-\tfrac{13}{2} = -6.5\)
1 \((1, 1)\) \((-1, -2)\) \((\tfrac{6}{5}, \tfrac{7}{5})\) \(-\tfrac{36}{5} = -7.2\)
2 \((\tfrac{6}{5}, \tfrac{7}{5})\) \((0, -1)\) \((\tfrac{6}{5}, \tfrac{8}{5})\) \(-\tfrac{184}{25} = -7.36\)

So \(x_3 = (1.2, 1.6)\) with \(f(x_3) = -7.36\), and the gap \(f(x_k) - f^*\) falls \(1 \to 0.3 \to 0.14\). Notice that the first coordinate overshoots its target 1 (reaching 1.2) and then waits for the second coordinate to catch up: the off-diagonal entry of \(A\) couples the two and bends the path.

(c) The eigenvalues of \(A\) are \(\lambda = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}\), about \(3.618\) and \(1.382\). Convergence from every start needs \(\eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\):

\[ \eta < \frac{4}{5 + \sqrt{5}} = 1 - \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \approx 0.553 . \]

The step \(\eta = 0.2\) is comfortably inside this range (see P8.9 for the proof).

Key insight: For \(f = \frac{1}{2}x^\top A x + b^\top x\) the minimiser is \(-A^{-1}b\), but gradient descent reaches it using only products with \(A\), at a speed set by the eigenvalues of \(A\).

P8.8 L2 · Computation

Exact line search on \(x^2 + 2y^2\)

Slide 290 minimises \(h(\gamma) = f\big(x - \gamma (\nabla f(x))^\top\big)\) at each step. Do the same for \(f(x, y) = x^2 + 2y^2\) from \((4, 1)\).

(a) Show that \(h(\gamma) = (1 - 2\gamma)^2 x^2 + 2(1 - 4\gamma)^2 y^2\) and that its minimiser is

\[ \gamma^* = \frac{x^2 + 4y^2}{2x^2 + 16y^2}. \]

(b) Take two exact-line-search steps from \((4, 1)\). Give each \(\gamma^*\), each new point and each value of \(f\).

(c) Check that consecutive gradients are orthogonal, and compare the direction of \(\nabla f\) at the third point with the first.

Hint

\(\nabla f = (2x, 4y)\), so the new point is \(\big((1 - 2\gamma)x,\ (1 - 4\gamma)y\big)\). Set \(h'(\gamma) = 0\) and solve the linear equation in \(\gamma\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Substituting the new point into \(f\) gives the stated \(h(\gamma)\). Differentiating,

\[ h'(\gamma) = -4(1 - 2\gamma)x^2 - 16(1 - 4\gamma)y^2 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 4x^2 + 16y^2 = \gamma\,(8x^2 + 64y^2), \]

which gives \(\gamma^* = \frac{x^2 + 4y^2}{2x^2 + 16y^2}\). Since \(h''(\gamma) = 8x^2 + 64y^2 > 0\), this is a minimum.

(b) Start: \(f(4, 1) = 18\), \(\nabla f = (8, 4)\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{Step 1:}\quad \gamma_1^* &= \frac{16 + 4}{32 + 16} = \frac{5}{12}, & (x_1, y_1) &= \big(4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{6},\ 1 \cdot (-\tfrac{2}{3})\big) = \big(\tfrac{2}{3}, -\tfrac{2}{3}\big), & f &= \tfrac{4}{3}, \\ \text{Step 2:}\quad \gamma_2^* &= \frac{\frac{4}{9} + \frac{16}{9}}{\frac{8}{9} + \frac{64}{9}} = \frac{5}{18}, & (x_2, y_2) &= \big(\tfrac{2}{3} \cdot \tfrac{4}{9},\ -\tfrac{2}{3} \cdot (-\tfrac{1}{9})\big) = \big(\tfrac{8}{27}, \tfrac{2}{27}\big), & f &= \tfrac{8}{81}. \end{aligned} \]

So \(\gamma_1^* = 5/12\), \(x_1 = (2/3, -2/3)\), \(f = 4/3\) and \(\gamma_2^* = 5/18\), \(x_2 = (8/27, 2/27)\), \(f = 8/81 \approx 0.0988\). Each step multiplies \(f\) by \(\tfrac{2}{27} \approx 0.074\).

(c) The gradients are \(g_0 = (8, 4)\), \(g_1 = (\tfrac{4}{3}, -\tfrac{8}{3})\) and \(g_2 = (\tfrac{16}{27}, \tfrac{8}{27})\):

\[ g_0 \cdot g_1 = \tfrac{32}{3} - \tfrac{32}{3} = 0, \qquad g_1 \cdot g_2 = \tfrac{64}{81} - \tfrac{64}{81} = 0 . \]

Consecutive gradients are orthogonal, and \(g_2 = \tfrac{2}{27}\, g_0\) is parallel to \(g_0\). The path therefore zig-zags between just two directions at right angles (the general proof is P8.23), and the step sizes alternate \(5/12, 5/18, 5/12, \dots\)

Key insight: Exact line search picks the best step along the current direction, which makes the new gradient perpendicular to the old one; on an elongated bowl this forces a right-angled zig-zag.

P8.9 L4 · Analysis

When does gradient descent on a quadratic converge?

Let \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^\top A x + b^\top x\) with \(A\) symmetric positive definite, eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_d > 0\) and orthonormal eigenvectors \(q_1, \dots, q_d\). Run \(x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta(\nabla f(x_k))^\top\) with a constant \(\eta > 0\).

(a) Show that the error \(e_k = x_k - x^*\) satisfies \(e_{k+1} = (I - \eta A)e_k\).

(b) Prove that \(x_k \to x^*\) for every \(x_0\) if and only if \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_i \rvert < 1\) for all \(i\), that is, \(0 < \eta < 2/\lambda_1\).

(c) Show that the error shrinks by the factor \(\rho(\eta) = \max_i \lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_i \rvert\) per step (in the eigen-coordinates), that the best constant step is \(\eta^* = 2/(\lambda_1 + \lambda_d)\), and that then \(\rho = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}\) with \(\kappa = \lambda_1/\lambda_d\).

(d) What breaks if \(A\) has a negative eigenvalue?

(e) Check (c) against P8.6 and P8.7.

Hint

Use \(Ax^* = -b\) for (a). For (b), write \(e_0 = \sum_i c_i q_i\) and note that \(q_i\) is an eigenvector of \(I - \eta A\) with eigenvalue \(1 - \eta\lambda_i\). For (c), \(\max\) of \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_1 \rvert\) and \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_d \rvert\) is smallest when they are equal.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \((\nabla f(x_k))^\top = Ax_k + b = Ax_k - Ax^* = Ae_k\). Subtracting \(x^*\) from the update,

\[ e_{k+1} = e_k - \eta A e_k = (I - \eta A)\, e_k . \]

(b) Expand \(e_0 = \sum_i c_i q_i\). Since \((I - \eta A)q_i = (1 - \eta\lambda_i)q_i\),

\[ e_k = (I - \eta A)^k e_0 = \sum_{i=1}^{d} c_i\, (1 - \eta\lambda_i)^k\, q_i, \qquad \lVert e_k \rVert^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{d} c_i^2\, (1 - \eta\lambda_i)^{2k}. \]

If: when every \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_i \rvert < 1\), each term tends to 0, so \(e_k \to 0\) for every \(e_0\).

Only if: if some \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_j \rvert \ge 1\), choose \(x_0 = x^* + q_j\). Then \(e_k = (1 - \eta\lambda_j)^k q_j\) has \(\lVert e_k \rVert = \lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_j \rvert^k \ge 1\) for all \(k\), so it never converges.

Finally, \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_i \rvert < 1 \iff 0 < \eta\lambda_i < 2\), and the binding case is the largest eigenvalue: \(0 < \eta < 2/\lambda_{\max}\).

(c) From the expansion, \(\lVert e_{k+1} \rVert \le \rho(\eta)\, \lVert e_k \rVert\) with \(\rho(\eta) = \max_i \lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_i \rvert\), and \(\rho\) is attained by an eigenvector. As a function of \(\eta\), \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_d \rvert\) decreases and \(\lvert 1 - \eta\lambda_1 \rvert\) increases once \(\eta > 1/\lambda_1\), so the maximum is smallest where \(1 - \eta\lambda_d = -(1 - \eta\lambda_1)\):

\[ \eta^* = \frac{2}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_d}, \qquad \rho^* = 1 - \frac{2\lambda_d}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_d} = \frac{\lambda_1 - \lambda_d}{\lambda_1 + \lambda_d} = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}. \]

Reducing the error by a factor \(\varepsilon\) takes about \(\ln(1/\varepsilon)/\ln\frac{\kappa + 1}{\kappa - 1} \approx \frac{\kappa}{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon)\) steps for large \(\kappa\): the iteration count grows linearly with the condition number.

(d) If \(\lambda_j < 0\), then \(1 - \eta\lambda_j > 1\) for every \(\eta > 0\), so the component along \(q_j\) grows geometrically: \(f\) is unbounded below in that direction (the stationary point is a saddle) and no step size makes the iteration converge, unless \(c_j = 0\) exactly.

(e) P8.6: \(\lambda = 8, 2\), \(\kappa = 4\), \(\eta^* = 2/10 = 0.2\), \(\rho^* = 3/5\), matching the factors \(\pm 0.6\) found there, and \(\eta < 0.25\) matching the divergence at \(\eta = 0.3\). P8.7: \(\lambda = \frac{5 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}\), \(\kappa = \frac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx 2.618\), \(\eta^* = 2/5\), \(\rho^* = \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \approx 0.447\).

Key insight: In the eigenbasis of the Hessian, gradient descent is \(d\) independent scalar iterations \(c \leftarrow (1 - \eta\lambda_i)c\); the largest eigenvalue limits the step and the ratio \(\kappa\) sets how many steps you need.

10.C Gradient Checking (8.3)

P8.10 L1 · Foundation

Finite-difference gradient checks: true or false

Slide 291 approximates \(\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_i} \approx \frac{J(w + \Delta e_i) - J(w)}{\Delta}\), where \(e_i\) is the \(i\)-th unit vector. Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "The forward difference above has error of order \(\Delta\), while the central difference \(\frac{J(w + \Delta e_i) - J(w - \Delta e_i)}{2\Delta}\) has error of order \(\Delta^2\)."

(b) "In floating-point arithmetic, making \(\Delta\) smaller always makes the estimate more accurate."

(c) "Finite differences are a cheaper replacement for backpropagation when training a large network."

(d) "The central difference gives the exact partial derivative of any quadratic function (apart from rounding)."

(e) "If the analytic and numerical gradients agree on the few coordinates you sampled, the whole analytic gradient is proven correct."

(f) "A relative error such as \(\frac{\lvert g_{\text{num}} - g_{\text{an}} \rvert}{\max(\lvert g_{\text{num}} \rvert, \lvert g_{\text{an}} \rvert)}\) is a better pass/fail measure than the absolute difference."

Hint

Expand \(J(w \pm \Delta e_i)\) by Taylor's theorem and see which terms cancel. For (b), remember that \(J(w + \Delta e_i)\) and \(J(w)\) are each stored with a relative rounding error of about \(10^{-16}\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. The forward error is \(\frac{1}{2}\frac{\partial^2 J}{\partial w_i^2}\Delta + O(\Delta^2)\); in the central difference the second-order terms cancel and the error is \(\frac{1}{6}\frac{\partial^3 J}{\partial w_i^3}\Delta^2 + O(\Delta^4)\) (P8.12).

(b) False. Subtracting two nearly equal numbers loses digits: the rounding error grows like \(10^{-16}/\Delta\). Below some \(\Delta\) (about \(10^{-8}\) for forward, \(10^{-5}\) for central differences) the estimate gets worse.

(c) False. One full numerical gradient costs \(d + 1\) (forward) or \(2d\) (central) evaluations of \(J\), against about one forward plus one backward pass for backpropagation. That is why slide 291 checks only a few sampled coordinates; finite differences are a test, not a training method.

(d) True. For a quadratic the third derivative is zero, so the truncation error of the central difference vanishes. (P8.13 exploits this.)

(e) False. The check is evidence, not proof: a bug in an unsampled coordinate, or one that happens to vanish at the test point, goes undetected.

(f) True. An absolute difference of \(10^{-4}\) is negligible if the gradient entry is \(10^{3}\) and alarming if it is \(10^{-4}\). A relative error is scale-free.

Key insight: Finite differences trade truncation error (which falls as \(\Delta\) shrinks) against rounding error (which grows as \(\Delta\) shrinks), and they are a cheap spot-check of an exact gradient, never a substitute for it.

P8.11 L2 · Computation

Forward and central differences side by side

Let \(J(w_1, w_2) = w_1^3 + 2w_1 w_2\) and \(w = (1, 1)\).

(a) Compute the exact gradient \(\nabla J(1, 1)\).

(b) Estimate \(\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_1}\) by the forward difference and by the central difference, each with \(\Delta = 0.1\) and \(\Delta = 0.01\). Give the error of each estimate.

(c) By what factor does each error shrink when \(\Delta\) is divided by 10? What does that tell you about the order of each method?

(d) Why do both methods give \(\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_2}\) exactly?

Hint

\(J(1.1, 1) = 1.331 + 2.2\) and \(J(0.9, 1) = 0.729 + 1.8\). Keep all decimals until the end.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) \(\nabla J = (3w_1^2 + 2w_2,\ 2w_1)\), so \(\nabla J(1, 1) = (5, 2)\).

(b) With \(J(1, 1) = 3\):

\[ \begin{aligned} \Delta = 0.1:&\quad \text{forward} = \frac{3.531 - 3}{0.1} = 5.31, \qquad \text{central} = \frac{3.531 - 2.529}{0.2} = 5.01, \\ \Delta = 0.01:&\quad \text{forward} = \frac{3.050301 - 3}{0.01} = 5.0301, \qquad \text{central} = \frac{3.050301 - 2.950299}{0.02} = 5.0001 . \end{aligned} \]

\(\Delta\) forward error central error
0.1 5.31 0.31 5.01 0.01
0.01 5.0301 0.0301 5.0001 0.0001

(c) The forward error shrinks by about 10 (0.31 to 0.0301), so it is first order, \(O(\Delta)\); its leading term is \(\frac{1}{2}J_{w_1 w_1}\Delta = \frac{1}{2}(6)(\Delta) = 3\Delta\). The central error shrinks by 100 (0.01 to 0.0001), so it is second order, \(O(\Delta^2)\); its error is exactly \(\frac{1}{6}J_{w_1 w_1 w_1}\Delta^2 = \frac{1}{6}(6)\Delta^2 = \Delta^2\).

(d) \(J\) is linear in \(w_2\) (\(J = \text{const} + 2w_1 w_2\)), so every difference quotient in \(w_2\) equals the slope \(2w_1 = 2\) exactly: all higher derivatives in \(w_2\) are zero.

Key insight: Doing one extra function evaluation to centre the difference buys a whole order of accuracy, so the central difference with a moderate \(\Delta\) is the standard tool for gradient checking.

P8.12 L4 · Analysis

Error orders and the best \(\Delta\)

Let \(\phi(t) = J(w + t e_i)\), so \(\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_i}(w) = \phi'(0)\). Assume \(\phi\) has continuous derivatives up to order 3 near 0, with \(\lvert \phi'' \rvert \le M_2\) and \(\lvert \phi''' \rvert \le M_3\).

(a) Use Taylor's theorem to show that the forward difference \(D_+ = \frac{\phi(\Delta) - \phi(0)}{\Delta}\) has error \(\frac{1}{2}\phi''(\xi)\Delta\) for some \(\xi \in (0, \Delta)\).

(b) Show that the central difference \(D_c = \frac{\phi(\Delta) - \phi(-\Delta)}{2\Delta}\) has error at most \(\frac{M_3}{6}\Delta^2\).

(c) Suppose each computed value of \(\phi\) carries an absolute rounding error of at most \(\varepsilon\lvert\phi\rvert\), with \(\varepsilon \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}\) in double precision. Write a bound on the total error of each method, and find the \(\Delta\) that minimises it. Give the order of magnitude of the best \(\Delta\) and of the best achievable error, taking \(\lvert \phi \rvert\), \(M_2\) and \(M_3\) to be about 1.

Hint

For (b), expand \(\phi(\pm\Delta)\) to third order with a remainder and subtract; the even-order terms cancel. For (c), minimise \(a\Delta + c/\Delta\) and \(a\Delta^2 + c/\Delta\) by calculus.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder gives \(\phi(\Delta) = \phi(0) + \phi'(0)\Delta + \frac{1}{2}\phi''(\xi)\Delta^2\), so

\[ D_+ - \phi'(0) = \tfrac{1}{2}\phi''(\xi)\,\Delta, \qquad \lvert D_+ - \phi'(0) \rvert \le \tfrac{M_2}{2}\Delta = O(\Delta). \]

(b) Expanding both sides to third order,

\[ \phi(\pm\Delta) = \phi(0) \pm \phi'(0)\Delta + \tfrac{1}{2}\phi''(0)\Delta^2 \pm \tfrac{1}{6}\phi'''(\xi_\pm)\Delta^3 . \]

Subtracting, the \(\phi(0)\) and \(\phi''(0)\) terms cancel:

\[ D_c - \phi'(0) = \frac{\phi'''(\xi_+) + \phi'''(\xi_-)}{12}\,\Delta^2, \qquad \lvert D_c - \phi'(0) \rvert \le \frac{M_3}{6}\Delta^2 = O(\Delta^2). \]

(c) The numerator of each quotient carries a rounding error of at most \(2\varepsilon\lvert\phi\rvert\). Dividing by \(\Delta\) or \(2\Delta\):

\[ E_+(\Delta) \le \frac{M_2}{2}\Delta + \frac{2\varepsilon\lvert\phi\rvert}{\Delta}, \qquad E_c(\Delta) \le \frac{M_3}{6}\Delta^2 + \frac{\varepsilon\lvert\phi\rvert}{\Delta}. \]

Setting the derivatives to zero:

\[ \Delta_+^{\text{best}} = 2\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon\lvert\phi\rvert}{M_2}} \approx 3 \times 10^{-8}, \qquad \Delta_c^{\text{best}} = \Big(\frac{3\varepsilon\lvert\phi\rvert}{M_3}\Big)^{1/3} \approx 9 \times 10^{-6}. \]

So the best \(\Delta\) is of order \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\) for the forward difference and \(\varepsilon^{1/3}\) for the central one. The best errors are \(2\sqrt{M_2\varepsilon\lvert\phi\rvert} \approx 3 \times 10^{-8}\) (order \(\sqrt{\varepsilon}\)) for the forward difference and \(\frac{1}{2}(\Delta_c^{\text{best}})^2 \approx 4 \times 10^{-11}\) (order \(\varepsilon^{2/3}\)) for the central difference. So forward differences can never be trusted beyond about 8 digits, and central differences reach about 10–11 digits at a larger, safer \(\Delta\).

Key insight: The total error is a U-shaped function of \(\Delta\); the central difference has a lower and wider U, which is why gradient checks use it with \(\Delta\) around \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-4}\) rather than "as small as possible".

P8.13 L5 · Mastery

Debugging a ridge-regression gradient

A student fits ridge regression by minimising

\[ J(w) = \sum_{i=1}^{3} (w^\top x_i - y_i)^2 + \lambda \lVert w \rVert^2, \qquad \lambda = 1, \]

with rows \(x_1 = (1, 2)\), \(x_2 = (0, 1)\), \(x_3 = (1, -1)\) stacked in \(X\), and \(y = (3, 1, 0)\). Their code returns the gradient (as a column) \(2X^\top(Xw - y) + \lambda w\).

(a) At \(w = (2, -1)\) compute \(J(w)\), the correct gradient and the student's gradient.

(b) The loss values \(J(2.01, -1) = 27.0403\), \(J(1.99, -1) = 26.9603\), \(J(2, -0.99) = 26.7607\) and \(J(2, -1.01) = 27.2407\) are given. Form the central-difference estimate of each partial derivative with \(\Delta = 0.01\), and the relative error of the student's gradient in each coordinate. Which coordinate fails a tolerance of \(10^{-4}\)?

(c) Why can the central difference here be trusted to essentially all digits, even with \(\Delta = 0.01\)? What would the forward difference \(\frac{J(w + \Delta e_i) - J(w)}{\Delta}\) have given?

(d) Diagnose the bug from the pattern of the mismatch.

(e) The student first ran the check at \(w = 0\) and it passed. Explain why, and state two rules for choosing where to run a gradient check.

Hint

The correct gradient is \(2X^\top(Xw - y) + 2\lambda w\). At \(w = (2, -1)\) the residual vector is \(Xw - y = (-3, -2, 3)\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The residuals are \(Xw - y = (0, -1, 3) - (3, 1, 0) = (-3, -2, 3)\), so

\[ J(w) = 9 + 4 + 9 + (4 + 1) = 27, \qquad 2X^\top(Xw - y) = 2\begin{bmatrix} -3 + 0 + 3 \\ -6 - 2 - 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -22 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The correct gradient adds \(2\lambda w = (4, -2)\), giving \((4, -24)\). The student's gradient adds \(\lambda w = (2, -1)\), giving \((2, -23)\).

(b) The central differences are

\[ \frac{27.0403 - 26.9603}{0.02} = 4, \qquad \frac{26.7607 - 27.2407}{0.02} = -24 . \]

Relative errors of the student's entries: coordinate 1, \(\frac{\lvert 2 - 4 \rvert}{4} = 0.5\); coordinate 2, \(\frac{\lvert -23 + 24 \rvert}{24} \approx 0.042\). Both coordinates fail, the first one dramatically.

(c) \(J\) is quadratic in \(w\), so its third derivatives are zero and the central difference has no truncation error (P8.10 (d)); only rounding remains, around \(10^{-13}\) here. The forward difference has error \(\frac{1}{2}J_{w_i w_i}\Delta\), and the Hessian is \(2X^\top X + 2\lambda I = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 14 \end{bmatrix}\), so it would give \(4 + 0.03 = 4.03\) and \(-24 + 0.07 = -23.93\), with relative errors about \(0.0075\) and \(0.003\) even for a correct gradient. With a forward difference the tolerance must be much looser, and small bugs hide in the slack.

(d) The mismatch is correct \(-\) student \(= (2, -1) = \lambda w\): exactly one copy of \(\lambda w\) is missing. The derivative of \(\lambda\lVert w \rVert^2\) is \(2\lambda w\), not \(\lambda w\); the student dropped the factor 2 from the penalty term.

(e) At \(w = 0\) the penalty gradient \(2\lambda w\) is zero whatever the factor, so both versions return \(2X^\top(-y) = (-6, -14)\) and the check passes. Rules: check at a random, generic point (no zero or symmetric parameters, which can make terms vanish), and check each term of a composite loss separately or with its coefficient switched on (here \(\lambda \ne 0\) and \(w \ne 0\)). Checking a few random coordinates at a couple of random points, with a central difference and a relative-error tolerance, catches almost all such bugs.

Key insight: A gradient check is only as good as the test point: bugs that multiply a vanishing quantity are invisible there, so check at generic points with the central difference and a relative tolerance.

10.D Learning-rate Schedules (8.4)

P8.14 L1 · Foundation

Schedules and the bold driver: true or false

Answer true or false, with a one-line reason for each.

(a) "With a large constant learning rate the iterates can get near the optimum quickly and then keep oscillating around it, while a small constant rate converges very slowly."

(b) "Exponential decay \(\alpha_t = \alpha_0 e^{-kt}\) and inverse decay \(\alpha_t = \alpha_0/(1 + kt)\) shrink at about the same speed for large \(t\)."

(c) "In the deck, \(t\) counts epochs (passes over the whole training set), so the learning rate is constant within one epoch."

(d) "Step decay multiplies the learning rate by a fixed factor, such as \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), every few epochs."

(e) "The bold-driver algorithm raises the rate by about 5% after every improving step, and after a worsening step it undoes the step and halves the rate."

(f) "The bold driver works just as well when the objective is estimated from a random mini-batch at every step."

Hint

For (b), compare \(e^{-kt}\) with \(1/(1 + kt)\) at \(t = 10\) and \(k = 0.5\). For (f), ask what "the objective worsened" means if the objective itself is a noisy estimate.

Answer & Key Insight

(a) True. This is slide 292's motivation. With noisy (stochastic) gradients a large constant rate leaves the iterates bouncing in a region around the optimum whose size grows with the rate; even with exact gradients, a rate between \(1/\lambda_{\max}\) and \(2/\lambda_{\max}\) overshoots on every step (P8.5). A small rate is stable but takes many steps.

(b) False. Exponential decay is far faster: at \(k = 0.5\), \(t = 10\), \(e^{-5} \approx 0.0067\) while \(1/(1 + 5) \approx 0.167\), a factor of about 25. Exponential decay can shrink the rate so quickly that training stops before reaching the optimum (P8.17).

(c) True. Slide 293 measures \(t\) in cycles over all training points and keeps the rate fixed during a cycle.

(d) True. That is slide 294's step decay: a piecewise-constant schedule such as halving every 2 epochs.

(e) True. Slide 295 gives these factors (+5% on success; undo and \(-50\%\) on failure).

(f) False. Slide 295 warns about this: with a sampled objective, an apparent "worsening" may be sampling noise, so the rate is cut for no reason (or raised on a lucky batch). Slide 296 suggests judging the objective over \(m\) steps instead of one.

Key insight: A schedule should take big steps early and small steps late; how fast it decays decides whether the run settles at the optimum, stalls short of it, or keeps bouncing.

P8.15 L2 · Computation

Three decay schedules by the numbers

Take \(\alpha_0 = 0.1\) and \(k = 0.5\).

(a) Tabulate, for \(t = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 10\): exponential decay \(\alpha_0 e^{-kt}\), inverse decay \(\alpha_0/(1 + kt)\), and step decay that halves the rate every 2 epochs, \(\alpha_0 (\tfrac{1}{2})^{\lfloor t/2 \rfloor}\).

(b) After how many epochs does each schedule first fall below \(0.01\)?

(c) The total of all the rates, \(\sum_{t \ge 0} \alpha_t\), bounds how far the parameters can travel when the gradient has norm at most 1. Compute it for each schedule (or show it is infinite).

Hint

The exponential and step schedules are geometric series. The inverse schedule behaves like \(\frac{0.2}{t}\) for large \(t\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) Rounded to four significant figures:

\(t\) exponential inverse step (halve every 2)
0 0.1 0.1 0.1
1 0.06065 0.06667 0.1
2 0.03679 0.05 0.05
3 0.02231 0.04 0.05
4 0.01353 0.03333 0.025
10 0.000674 0.01667 0.003125

(b) Exponential: \(0.1e^{-0.5t} < 0.01 \iff t > 2\ln 10 \approx 4.61\), so \(t = 5\) (\(\alpha_5 \approx 0.0082\)). Inverse: \(0.1/(1 + 0.5t) < 0.01 \iff t > 18\), so \(t = 19\). Step: \(0.1 \cdot 2^{-\lfloor t/2 \rfloor} < 0.01\) needs \(\lfloor t/2 \rfloor \ge 4\), so \(t = 8\) (\(\alpha_8 = 0.00625\)).

(c) Exponential:

\[ \sum_{t \ge 0} 0.1 e^{-0.5t} = \frac{0.1}{1 - e^{-0.5}} \approx 0.254 . \]

Step decay: each rate is used for two epochs, so \(\sum = 2(0.1 + 0.05 + 0.025 + \dots) = 2 \cdot \frac{0.1}{1 - 1/2} = 0.4\). Inverse decay: \(\sum_t \frac{0.1}{1 + 0.5t} = \sum_t \frac{0.2}{t + 2}\) is a tail of the harmonic series, so it is infinite (it reaches about 0.84 after 100 epochs and 1.76 after 10 000, growing like \(0.2\ln t\)).

So exponential and step decay have a finite "travel budget" (0.254 and 0.4), while inverse decay has an unlimited one. If the optimum is farther away than the budget allows, the first two schedules stop short of it.

Key insight: The shape of a schedule matters as much as its starting value: geometric schedules give a finite total step length, while \(1/t\)-type schedules can still reach any point eventually.

P8.16 L3 · Application

The bold driver finds the stability edge

Minimise \(f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^2\) from \(x_0 = 10\) with the bold-driver rule: after an attempted step \(x \leftarrow x - \eta f'(x)\), if \(f\) decreased, keep the step and set \(\eta \leftarrow 1.05\eta\); otherwise undo the step and set \(\eta \leftarrow 0.5\eta\). Start with \(\eta_0 = 1.9\).

(a) Show that an accepted step multiplies \(x\) by \(1 - \eta\), and state which \(\eta\) decrease \(f\).

(b) Carry out the first five attempted steps. For each, record \(\eta\), the trial point, its \(f\), and whether it is accepted. (Keep four or more significant figures.)

(c) Explain what the bold driver "discovered" about this problem in steps 1–4.

Hint

\(f'(x) = x\), so the trial point is \((1 - \eta)x\), and \(f\) decreases exactly when \(\lvert 1 - \eta \rvert < 1\).

Answer & Key Insight

(a) The trial point is \(x - \eta x = (1 - \eta)x\), so \(f\) is multiplied by \((1 - \eta)^2\). \(f\) decreases if and only if \(0 < \eta < 2\), and \(\eta = 1\) jumps straight to the minimum.

(b) Starting from \(x = 10\), \(f = 50\):

attempt \(\eta\) trial \(x\) trial \(f\) decision next \(\eta\)
1 1.9 \(-9\) 40.5 accept 1.995
2 1.995 8.955 40.10 accept 2.09475
3 2.09475 \(-9.8035\) 48.05 reject, stay at 8.955 1.047375
4 1.047375 \(-0.42424\) 0.08999 accept 1.09974
5 1.09974 0.042316 0.000895 accept 1.15473

(c) Steps 1 and 2 use \(\eta\) close to the stability limit \(\eta = 2 = 2/f''\), so \(x\) just flips sign and \(f\) barely falls (50, 40.5, 40.1).
